chapters.title: Dedication
paragraphs: You approach again, you wavering forms, who once, in the morning of life, presented yourselves to my troubled view! Shall I try, this time, to hold you fast? Do I feel my heart still drawn to that illusion? You crowd around me! Very well then, you may hold dominion over me, as you rise out of vapor and mist. My breast feels youthfully stirred by the magic breath that surrounds your train. You bring with you the images of happy days, and many beloved shades arise: like an old, half-forgotten tradition, first love comes back with friendship in its company. The pang is renewed; the lament traces again the labyrinthine course of life, and names the dear ones who, cheated of their fair hours by fate, have vanished before me. They cannot hear the songs that follow — those souls to whom I sang my first. Scattered is the friendly throng — the first echo, alas, has died away! My sorrow now resounds among a strange crowd: their very applause saddens my heart, and those who were once gladdened by my song — if they are still living — wander scattered through the world. And a yearning, long unfelt, for that quiet, pensive spirit-realm seizes me. In half-formed tones my faltering song hovers like an Aeolian harp. A tremor takes hold of me: tear follows tear; the austere heart feels itself growing mild and soft. What I have, I see as if in the distance; and what is gone becomes real to me.

chapters.title: Prelude on the Stage
paragraphs: MANAGER — THEATRE-POET — MERRYMAN.

MANAGER. You two, who have so often stood by me in need and trouble, tell me: what hopes do you have for our venture in German lands? I very much want to please the crowd, especially because they live and let live. The posts and boards are up, and everyone is looking forward to a feast. There they sit already, cool, with raised eyebrows, hoping to be made to wonder. I know how to win over the public spirit; yet I have never been in such a fix as now. They are not used to the best, true, but they have read a terrible amount. How shall we manage it — so that everything is fresh and new, and still pleasing and instructive? I do love to see the crowd, when the stream rushes toward our booth, and with powerfully repeated efforts forces itself through the narrow gate of grace — when, in broad daylight, before four o'clock, they elbow their way to the box office, and risk breaking their necks for a ticket, as though it were a famine at a baker's door for bread. It is the poet alone who works this miracle on such a motley crowd. My friend, oh, do it today!

POET. Oh, do not speak to me of that motley crowd, at the very sight of which one's spirit takes flight. Veil that surging throng from me, which draws us, against our will, into the whirlpool. No! lead me instead to the quiet, heavenly nook where pure enjoyment alone blooms for the poet — where love and friendship, with godlike hand, create and cherish the bliss of our hearts. Ah! what has gushed up there from the depths of the breast, what the lip coyly whispered to itself — now failing, now perhaps succeeding — the wild moment's force swallows it up. Often, only when it has endured through ages does it appear in its complete form. What glitters is born for the moment; the genuine remains undimmed for posterity.

MERRYMAN. If only I could hear no more about posterity! Suppose I chose to talk about posterity — who then would make fun for our contemporaries? They want fun, and they ought to have it. The presence of a good fellow, too, is worth something, I should think. Whoever knows how to share himself agreeably will never be soured by the public's caprice. He wants a large circle, the more surely to stir it. Then do your best, and show yourself a model. Let fancy with all her choruses — reason, understanding, feeling, passion — all be heard, but, mark me well, not without folly.

MANAGER. But, most particularly, let there be incident enough! People come to look; what they like best is to see. If much is spun out before their eyes, so that the crowd can gape in astonishment, you have already won by sheer abundance; you are a beloved man. You can only subdue the mass by mass. Each person eventually picks out something for himself. Whoever brings much will bring something to many a one, and all leave the house content. If you give a piece, give it at once in pieces! Such a stew is sure to succeed. It is as easily served as invented. What use is it to present a whole? The public will pull it to pieces for you anyway.
POET. You do not feel the baseness of such a trade; how little it becomes the true artist! The bungling of these fine gentlemen has already become a maxim with you, I see.

MANAGER. Such a reproof does not bother me at all. A man who intends to do real work must look out for the best tool. Consider, you have soft wood to split; and only look at whom you are writing for! One is driven by boredom, another comes over-stuffed from a meal of too many dishes; and worst of all, many a one comes from reading the newspapers. People hurry to us distractedly, as to a masquerade; curiosity alone wings every step. The ladies offer themselves and their finery as a treat, and play along with us without pay. What are you dreaming about, up on your poetic height? What is it that makes a full house merry? Look closely at your patrons! Half are indifferent, half coarse. One hopes for a game of cards after the play; another for a wild night in the arms of a girl. Why, poor fools that you are, do you give the sweet Muses so much trouble for such an end? I tell you, only give more, and more, and more again; that way you can never miss your mark. Try only to mystify the people; satisfying them is hard. What is coming over you? Delight or pain?

POET. Be gone — and find yourself another servant! Is the poet, really, to gamble away for your sake the highest right, the right of man, which Nature bestows on him? By what does he stir every heart? By what means does he subdue every element? Is it not the harmony that bursts forth from his breast, and draws the world back again into his heart? When Nature, carelessly winding, forces the thread's endless length upon the spindle; when the confused multitude of all beings jangles out of tune and harsh — who, life-infusing, so orders the ever evenly flowing series that it moves rhythmically? Who summons the individual to the general consecration, where it strikes in glorious harmony? Who bids the tempest rage into passions? the evening-red glow in the pensive spirit? Who scatters on the loved one's path all the beautiful blossoms of spring? Who weaves meaningless green leaves into a garland of honor for deserts of every kind? Who secures Olympus? — unites the gods? Man's power revealed in the poet.

MERRYMAN. Then put those fine powers to work, and run your poetical affairs as one runs a love-adventure. By chance one approaches, one feels, one stays, and little by little one gets entangled. Happiness grows — then it is disturbed; one is delighted — then comes distress; and before one is aware of it, it is even a romance. Let us also give a play in this manner. Just reach into the thick of human life! Everyone lives it — not many know it; and wherever you seize it, it is interesting. Little clearness amid motley images! Much falsehood and a spark of truth! That is the way to brew the best potion, one that refreshes and edifies the whole world. Then the fairest flower of youth gathers to see your play, and listens to the revelation. Then every gentle mind draws melancholy nourishment for itself out of your work; then now this, now that is stirred up; each one sees what he carries in his own heart. They are as ready to weep as to laugh; they still honor the soaring, are pleased with the glitter. There is no pleasing one who is already formed; one who is still forming will always be grateful.

POET. Then give me back the times when I myself was still forming — when a fountain of crowding songs sprang fresh and unbroken; when mists veiled the world before me, when the bud still promised marvels; when I gathered the thousand flowers that profusely filled every valley! I had nothing, and yet enough — the longing for truth, and the pleasure in illusion! Give me back those untamed impulses — the deep, pain-fraught happiness, the energy of hate, the power of love! Give me back my youth!

MERRYMAN. Youth, my good friend, you do need — when enemies press you hard in the fight, when lovely girls cling ardently around your neck, when from afar the garland of the swift race beckons from the hard-won goal, when, after the dance's maddening whirl, one drinks away the night carousing. But to strike the familiar lyre with spirit and grace, to sweep along with happy wanderings toward a self-appointed aim — that, old gentlemen, is your duty, and we honor you no less for it. Old age does not make childish, as people say; it only finds us still true children.

MANAGER. Words enough have been exchanged; let me now see deeds as well. While you are turning compliments, something useful might be done. What good does it do to stand talking about being in the mood? The hesitater never is. If you once give yourselves out as poets, then command poetry. You well know what we want; we want to sip strong drink — now brew away at once! What is not done today will not be done tomorrow; and no day should be wasted. Resolve should boldly seize the possible by the forelock at once. It will not then let go, and works on, because it must.

chapters.title: Prologue in Heaven
paragraphs: THE LORD — THE HEAVENLY HOSTS. Afterwards Mephistopheles.

RAPHAEL. The sun rings out, as ever, with the rival music of his brother spheres, and performs his prescribed journey with thundering march. The sight of him gives strength to the angels, though none can fathom him; your inconceivably sublime works are glorious as on the first day. GABRIEL. And swift, inconceivably swift, the splendor of the earth revolves; the brightness of paradise alternates with deep, fearful night. The sea foams up in broad waves at the deep base of the rocks; and rock and sea are whirled on in the ever-swift course of the spheres.

MICHAEL. And storms are roaring as if in rivalry, from sea to land, from land to sea, and form all around a chain of the deepest force in their rage. There, flashing desolation flares before the path of the thunderclap. But your messengers, Lord, revere the gentle movement of your day.
THE THREE. The sight gives strength to the angels, though none can fathom you, and all your sublime works are glorious as on the first day.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Since, Lord, you approach us once again, and ask how things are going with us, and have on other occasions usually not been displeased to see me — that is why you see me here among your retinue. Forgive me, I cannot talk fine, not though the whole circle should jeer at me. My pathos would certainly make you laugh, if you had not given up laughing. I have nothing to say about suns and worlds; I only notice how men torment themselves. The little god of the world stays ever of the same stamp, and is as odd as on the first day. He would lead a somewhat more pleasant life if you had not given him a glimmer of heaven's light. He calls it reason, and uses it only to be more brutal than any brute. He seems to me, with your Grace's leave, like one of those long-legged grasshoppers that is always flying, and leaping as it flies, and then sings its old song in the grass — and I wish he would just stay in the grass! He thrusts his nose into every puddle.
THE LORD. Have you nothing else to say to me? Do you always come for no other purpose than to complain? Is nothing ever to your liking on earth?
MEPHISTOPHELES. No, Lord! I find things there, as ever, miserably bad. Men in their days of wretchedness move my pity; even I myself have not the heart to torment the poor things.
THE LORD. Do you know Faust? MEPHISTOPHELES. The Doctor?
THE LORD. My servant!

MEPHISTOPHELES. Truly! he serves you in a strange fashion. The fool's meat and drink are not of earth. The ferment drives him toward the far away. He himself is half aware of his madness. From heaven he demands its brightest stars; from earth, its every highest enjoyment; and nothing near, and nothing far, satisfies his deeply agitated breast.
THE LORD. Although he serves me now only in confusion, I shall soon lead him into the light. When the tree buds, the gardener knows that blossom and fruit will adorn the coming years.
MEPHISTOPHELES. What will you wager? You will lose him yet, if you give me leave to guide him quietly down my own path.
THE LORD. So long as he lives upon the earth, you are not forbidden. Man errs as long as he strives.
MEPHISTOPHELES. I am much obliged to you for that; for I have never had any taste for the dead. I prefer plump, fresh cheeks. I am not at home to a corpse. I am like the cat with the mouse.

THE LORD. Enough, it is granted to you. Draw this spirit from his original source, and lead him down on your own path with you, if you can take hold of him. And stand ashamed, when you are forced to admit: a good man, in his groping strivings, still knows the right way.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Very well, very well — only it will not last long. I have no fear at all about my wager. If I succeed, excuse my triumphing with my whole soul. Dust he shall eat, and with relish, like my cousin, the famous snake.

THE LORD. There too you are free to act as you like. I have never hated your kind. Of all the spirits that deny, the rogue who jests is the least troublesome to me. Man's activity is all too prone to slacken; he soon grows fond of unbroken rest; I am therefore glad to give him a companion who stirs and works, and must, as devil, be doing something. But you, the true children of heaven, rejoice in the living abundance of beauty. May the creative essence, which works and lives through all time, embrace you within the happy bounds of love; and what hovers in changing semblance, fix firm with everlasting thoughts. [Heaven closes, the Archangels disperse.]

chapters.title: Night
paragraphs: FAUST. ... with bitter sweat, be forced to speak of what I do not know; that I may learn what holds the world together in its inmost core, see all the springs and seeds of production, and rummage no longer in empty words. Oh! that you, radiant moonlight, were looking for the last time upon my misery; you, for whom I have sat watching so many a midnight at this desk; then, over books and papers, melancholy friend, you appeared to me! Oh, that I might wander on the mountaintops in your beloved light — hover with spirits round the mountain caves — flit over the fields in your glimmer, and, unburdened of all the fumes of knowledge, bathe myself whole in your dew! Alas! am I still penned up in this dungeon? — accursed, musty, walled-in hole! — where even the precious light of heaven breaks mournfully through painted panes, choked by this heap of books, which worms eat, dust covers, which, up to the very top of the vault, a smoke-stained paper surrounds; with glasses, boxes ranged around, with instruments piled up on every side, ancestral lumber stuffed in among the rest. This is your world, and what a world! And do you still ask why your heart flutters anxiously in your breast? — why a vague aching deadens within you every stirring principle of life? — Instead of the living nature for which God made man, you have nothing around you but the skeletons of beasts and the bones of the dead, in smoke and mold. Up! away! Out into the wide world! And this mysterious book, from Nostradamus's own hand — is it not company enough for you? Then you will know the course of the stars, and, when nature instructs you, the soul's essence will rise up to you, as one spirit speaks to another. It is in vain that dull poring here expounds the holy signs to you! You are hovering, you Spirits, near me; answer me if you hear me. [He opens the book and sees the sign of the Macrocosm.] Ah! what rapture thrills all at once through every sense at this sight! I feel youthful, hallowed life-joy, newly glowing, shoot through nerve and vein. Was it a god who traced these signs, which still the storm within me, fill my poor heart with gladness, and, by a mystical intuition, unveil the powers of nature all around me? Am I a god? All grows so bright! In these pure lines I see Nature herself working in my soul's presence. Now for the first time I understand what the sage says — 'The spirit-world is not closed. Your sense is shut, your heart is dead! Up, acolyte! bathe, untiring, your earthly breast in the morning-red.'
[He contemplates the sign.]

How all weaves itself into a whole; one works and lives in the other. How heavenly powers ascend and descend, and reach each other the golden buckets — with bliss-exhaling wings, press from heaven through earth, all ringing harmoniously through the All. What a show! but ah, a show only! Where shall I grasp you, infinite Nature? You breasts, where? you sources of all life, on which heaven and earth hang, toward which the withered breast presses — you gush, you nourish, and am I to languish in vain? [He turns the page indignantly, and sees the sign of the Spirit of the Earth.] How differently this sign affects me! You, Spirit of the Earth, are nearer to me. Already I feel my energies raised, already I glow as with new wine; I feel the courage to venture into the world, to endure earthly joy, earthly pain, to wrestle with storms, and stand unshaken amid the shipwreck's crash. — Clouds thicken over me; the moon hides her light; the lamp dies away; vapors arise; red beams flash round my head; a cold shuddering flickers down from the vaulted roof and seizes me! I feel it — you are hovering round me, summoned Spirit. Unveil yourself! Ah! what a tearing in my heart — all my senses are stirred up to new sensations! I feel my whole heart surrendered to you. You must — you must! — though it cost me my life. [He seizes the book and mystically pronounces the sign of the Spirit. A red flame flashes up; the SPIRIT appears in the flame.]
SPIRIT. Who calls me?
FAUST (AVERTING HIS FACE). Horrible vision!
SPIRIT. You have compelled me here, have long been drawing on my sphere. And now —
FAUST. Woe is me! I cannot endure you.

SPIRIT. You pray, gasping, to see me, to hear my voice, to look upon my face. Your powerful invocation works upon me. I am here! What pitiful terror seizes you, the demigod! Where is the soul's call? Where is the breast that created a world within itself, and bore and cherished it? — which, with tremors of delight, swelled to lift itself up to a level with us, the Spirits. Where are you, Faust? whose voice rang to me, who pressed toward me with all his energies? Are you he? you, who, at the bare touch of my breath, are shivering through every depth of life, a trembling, writhing worm?
FAUST. Shall I yield to you, thing of flame? I am he, am Faust, your equal.

SPIRIT. In the tides of life, in action's storm, I am tossed up and down, I drift here and there. Birth and grave, an eternal sea, a changeful weaving, a glowing life — thus I work at the whirring loom of time, and weave the living garment of the Deity.
FAUST. Busy spirit, you who sweep round the wide world, how near I feel to you!
SPIRIT. You are like the Spirit you comprehend, not like me. [The Spirit vanishes.]

FAUST (COLLAPSING). Not you? Whom, then? I, the image of the Deity, and not even like you! [A knocking at the door.] Oh, death! I know it — that is my famulus — my fairest happiness is brought to nothing. That the pedantic plodder must disturb this fullness of visions! [WAGNER enters in his dressing gown and nightcap, with a lamp in his hand. FAUST turns away in displeasure.]

WAGNER. Excuse me — I hear you declaiming; surely you were reading a Greek tragedy? I should like to improve myself in this art, for nowadays it has considerable influence. I have often heard it said that an actor might instruct a preacher.
FAUST. Yes, when the preacher is an actor, as may well enough happen now and then.
WAGNER. Ah! when a man is so confined to his study, and barely sees the world on a holiday — barely through a telescope, only from afar — how is he to lead it by persuasion?

FAUST. If you do not feel it, you will not get it by hunting for it — if it does not gush from the soul, and subdue the hearts of all listeners with powerful delight. Sit at it forever — glue together — cook up a hash from the feast of others, and blow paltry flames out of your own little heap of ashes! You may gain the admiration of children and apes, if you have a taste for it; but you will never touch the hearts of others, if it does not flow fresh from your own.
WAGNER. But it is delivery that makes the orator's success. I feel well enough that I am still far behind.

FAUST. Seek honest gain only! Be no fool with loud, jingling bells! Reason and good sense are expressed with little art. And when you are seriously intent on saying something, is it necessary to hunt for words? Yes, your speeches, so glittering, in which you crisp the shreds of humanity, are as unrefreshing as the mist-wind rustling through the withered leaves in autumn.

WAGNER. Oh God, art is long, and our life is short. Often, in my critical studies, I feel oppressed both in head and heart. How hard it is to get hold of the means by which one climbs to the fountainhead; and before he has gone halfway, a poor devil must probably die!
FAUST. Is parchment the holy well, a drink from which quenches the thirst forever? You have not gained refreshment, if it does not gush from your own soul.
WAGNER. Excuse me! It is a great pleasure to transport oneself into the spirit of the times; to see how a wise man thought before us, and to what a glorious height we have at last carried it.

FAUST. Oh, yes — up to the very stars. My friend, past ages are to us a book with seven seals. What you call the spirit of the times is at bottom only your own spirit, in which the times are reflected. A miserable exhibition, too, it often is! One runs away from it at the first glance! A dust-barrel and a lumber-room! — and, at best, a heroic play, with fine pragmatic platitudes such as may suit the mouths of puppets!
WAGNER. But the world! The heart and mind of man! Everyone would like to know something about that.

FAUST. Yes, what is called knowing! Who dares call the child by its true name? The few who have ever known anything about it, who foolishly enough did not keep guard over their full hearts, who revealed what they had felt and seen to the multitude — these, from time immemorial, have been crucified and burned. Please, friend — the night is far advanced — for now we must break off.

WAGNER. I could gladly have stayed awake to converse with you so learnedly. Tomorrow, however, on Easter Day, permit me a question or two more. Zealously have I devoted myself to study. True, I know much; but I would like to know all. [Exit.]

FAUST (ALONE). How strange that all hope has not been lost to this brain that clings persistently to trash — that gropes with greedy hand for treasure, and exults at finding earthworms! Dare such a human voice sound here, where all around me teemed with spirits? Yet ah, this once I thank you, you poorest of all the sons of earth. You snatched me from the despair that threatened to destroy my reason. Alas! the vision was so giant-great, that I must feel like a dwarf. I, formed in God's own image, who already thought myself near the mirror of eternal truth; who reveled in heaven's brightness and clarity, with the earthly part of me stripped off; I, more than cherub, whose free spirit already, in its imaginative soarings, aspired to glide through nature's veins, and, in creating, enjoy the life of gods — how must I atone for it! A thunder-word has swept me far away. I dare not presume to compare myself with you. If I had the power to draw you to me, I had no power to hold you. In that blessed moment, I felt so small, so great; cruelly you thrust me back upon the uncertain lot of humanity. Who will teach me? What am I to shun? Must I obey that impulse? Alas! our actions, like our sufferings, clog the course of our lives. Something foreign, and ever more foreign, is always clinging to the noblest conception the mind can form. When we have attained to the good of this world, what is better is called deception and illusion. The glorious feelings that gave us life grow torpid in the worldly bustle. If imagination once, on daring wing and full of hope, dilated to infinity — a little space is now enough for it, when venture after venture has been wrecked in the whirlpool of time. Care nestles straight in the depths of the heart, hatches vague tortures there, rocks herself restlessly, and frightens joy and peace away. She is ever putting on new masks; she may appear as house and land, as wife and child, as fire, water, dagger and poison. You tremble before all that does not befall you, and must be always wailing what you never lose. I am not like the godheads; I feel it only too deeply. I am like the worm, which drags itself through the dust — which, as it seeks its living in the dust, is crushed and buried under the step of the passerby. Is it not dust, all that in a hundred shelves narrows this lofty wall? The lumber which, with thousandfold frippery, oppresses me in this moth-world? Here shall I find what I want? Am I to go on reading in a thousand books that men have toiled everywhere, that now and then there has been a happy one? You, hollow skull, what do you mean by that grin? but that your brain, like mine, once bewildered, sought the bright day, and, with an ardent longing for truth, went miserably astray in the twilight? You instruments are surely mocking me, with your wheels and cogs, cylinders and bows. I stood at the gate, you were to be the key; true, your wards are curiously twisted, but you do not raise the bolt. Inscrutable at broad day, Nature does not let herself be robbed of her veil; and what she does not choose to reveal to your mind, you will not wrest from her by levers and screws. You, antiquated lumber I have never used, you are here only because my father used you. You, old scroll, have been growing smoke-stained since the dim lamp first smouldered at this desk. Far better would it be for me to have squandered away the little I possess, than to be sweating here under the burden of that little. What you have inherited from your fathers, possess it in order to enjoy it. What one does not make use of is an oppressive burden; what the moment brings forth, that only can it profit by. But why are my eyes fastened on that spot: is that phial a magnet to my eyes? Why, of a sudden, is everything so exquisitely bright, as when in the wood at night moonlight surrounds us? I hail you, precious phial, which I now take down with reverence; in you I honor the wit and art of man. You essence of soothing soporific juices, you concentration of all refined deadly powers, show your favor to your master! I see you, and the pang is eased; I grasp you, and the struggle abates; the spirit's flood-tide ebbs by degrees. I am beckoned out into the wide sea; the glassy flood glitters at my feet; another day invites me to other shores. A chariot of fire floats, on light wings, down to me. I feel prepared to break through the realms of space, on a new track, to new spheres of pure activity. This sublime existence, this godlike beatitude — do you, worm just now, do you merit it? Yes — only resolutely turn your back on the lovely sun of this earth! Dare to tear open the gates which everyone gladly slinks past! Now is the time to show by deeds that man's dignity does not yield to divine sublimity — not to quail in the presence of that dark abyss, in which fantasy damns itself to its own torments — to struggle onward to that pass, round whose narrow mouth all hell is flaming; calmly to resolve upon the step, even at the risk of dropping into nothingness. Now come down, pure crystal goblet, which I have not thought of for many a year — come forth from your old case! You glittered at my ancestors' festivities; you gladdened the solemn guests, as one passed you to the other. The gorgeousness of the many artfully wrought images, the drinker's duty to explain them in rhyme, to empty the contents at one draught, reminds me of many a night of my youth. I shall not now pass you to a neighbor; I shall not now display my wit on your ... CHORUS OF DISCIPLES. Ah! on earth's bosom are we for suffering here! He left us, his own, languishing here below! Alas! we weep over, Master, your happy lot! CHORUS OF ANGELS. Christ is arisen out of corruption's lap. Joyfully tear yourselves loose from your bonds! You, in deeds giving praise to him, love manifesting, breaking bread brother-like, journeying and preaching him, bliss promising — to you the Master is near, for you he is here!

chapters.title: Before the Gate
paragraphs: Promenaders of all kinds pass out. SOME MECHANICS. Why that way? OTHERS. We are going to the mill. A MECHANIC. I advise you to go to the Wasserhof. A SECOND. The road is not at all pleasant. THE OTHERS. And what will you do then? A THIRD. I am going with the others. A FOURTH. Come up to Burghdorf; you are sure of finding the prettiest girls and the best beer there, and brawls of the first order. A FIFTH. You wild fellow, is your skin itching for the third time? I do not like going there; I have a horror of the place. SERVANT-GIRL. No, no, I shall return to the town. ANOTHER. We shall find him for certain by those poplars. THE FIRST. That is no great gain for me. He will walk by your side. With you alone does he dance on the green. What have I to do with your pleasures? THE SECOND. He is sure not to be alone today. The curly-head, he said, would be with him.

STUDENT. Zounds! how the buxom wenches step out; come along, brother, we must go with them. Strong beer, stinging tobacco, and a servant-girl in full trim — that is my taste. CITIZEN'S DAUGHTER. Now just look at those fine lads! It is really a shame. They could have the best of company, and instead are running after these servant-girls. SECOND STUDENT to the FIRST. Not so fast! Two are coming up behind; they are trimly dressed. One of them is my neighbor; I have quite a liking for the girl. They walk in their quiet way, and yet will let us join them in the end. THE FIRST. No, brother. I do not like being under restraint. Quick, before we lose the game. The hand that wields the broom on Saturdays will fondle you best on Sundays. BURGHER. No, the new Burgomaster is not to my taste; now that he has the post, he grows daily bolder; and what is he doing for the town? Is it not getting worse every day? One is forced to submit to more restraints than ever, and pay more than at any time before. BEGGAR (sings). You good gentlemen, you lovely ladies, so trimly dressed and rosy-cheeked, please look upon me, regard and relieve my wants. Do not let me sing here in vain. Only the free-handed are light-hearted. Let the day that is a holiday to all be a harvest-day to me. ANOTHER BURGHER. I know nothing better on Sundays and holidays than a chat about war and war's alarms, when people are fighting far away in Turkey. A man stands at his window, drinks a glass, and sees the painted vessels glide down the river; then goes home glad at heart in the evening, and blesses peace and times of peace. THIRD BURGHER. Yes, neighbor, I have no objection to that; let them break one another's heads and turn everything upside down, for all I care; only let things at home stay as they are. AN OLD WOMAN to the CITIZENS' DAUGHTERS. Hey-day! How smart! The pretty young creatures. Who would not be smitten with you? Only not so proud! it is all very well; and what you wish I could undertake to get for you. CITIZEN'S DAUGHTER. Come along, Agatha. I take care not to be seen with such witches in public; true, on Saint Andrew's Eve she showed me my future sweetheart in flesh and blood. THE OTHER. She showed me mine in the crystal, soldier-like, with other bold fellows; I look around, I seek him everywhere, but I can never meet him. SOLDIER. Towns with lofty walls and battlements, maidens with proud, scornful thoughts — I would gladly win. Bold the venture, noble the reward. And the trumpets are our summoners, to joy as to death. That is a storming, that is a life for you! Maidens and towns must surrender. Bold the venture, noble the reward — and the soldiers are off. [Enter FAUST and WAGNER.]

FAUST. River and rivulet are freed from ice by the gay quickening glance of spring; the joys of hope are budding in the valley; old winter, in his weakness, has retreated to the bleak mountains. From there he sends, in his flight, nothing but impotent showers of hail, in streaks, over the green-growing meadows. But the Sun endures no white. Production and growth are stirring everywhere; he wants to enliven everything with colors; the landscape wants flowers, so he takes gaily dressed men and women instead. Turn and look back from this rising ground at the town. Out of the gloomy gate presses a motley crowd. Everyone suns himself so willingly today. They celebrate the rising of the Lord, for they themselves have risen — from the damp rooms of mean houses, from the bondage of trade and industry, from the confinement of gables and roofs, from the stifling narrowness of streets, from the venerable gloom of churches, they are all raised up to the open light of day. But look, look! how quickly the crowd scatters through the gardens and fields; how the river, in breadth and length, tosses many a merry boat upon its surface; how this last skiff, overladen almost to sinking, moves off. Even from the farthest mountain paths, gay-colored dresses flash at us. I hear already the bustle of the village; here is the true heaven of the multitude; big and little are huzzaing joyously. Here, I am a man — here, I may be one.

WAGNER. To walk with you, Sir Doctor, is honor and profit; but I would not lose myself here alone, because I am an enemy to coarseness of every sort. This fiddling, shouting, skittle-playing — these are sounds thoroughly detestable to me. People run riot as if the devil were driving them, and call it merriment, call it singing. RUSTICS UNDER THE LIME-TREE. DANCE AND SONG. The shepherd dressed himself out for the dance, with party-colored jacket, ribbon and garland — smartly was he dressed! The ring round the lime-tree was already full, and all were dancing like mad. Huzza! Huzza! Tira-lira-hara-la! Merrily went the fiddle-stick. He pressed eagerly in, gave a maiden a push with his elbow: the buxom girl turned round and said — Now that I call stupid. Huzza! Huzza! Tira-lira-hara-la! Don't be so ill-bred. Yet nimbly it sped in the ring; they turned right, they turned left, and all the petticoats were flying. They grew red, they grew warm, and rested panting arm in arm. Huzza! Huzza! Tira-lira-hara-la! And elbow on hip — Have done now! Don't be so familiar! How many a man has cajoled and deceived his betrothed. But he coaxed her aside, and far and wide echoed from the lime-tree, Huzza! Huzza! Tira-lira-hara-la! Shouts and fiddle-sticks.

OLD PEASANT. Doctor, this is really good of you, not to scorn us today, and, great scholar as you are, to mingle in this crowd. Take then the fairest jug, which we have filled with fresh drink. I pledge you in it, and pray aloud that it may not only quench your thirst — may the number of drops it holds be added to your days!
FAUST. I accept the refreshing draught, and wish you all health and happiness in return.
[The people gather round him.]

OLD PEASANT. Truly it is well done of you, to appear on this glad day; you who have been our friend in evil days before. Many a one stands here alive whom your father tore from the rage of hot fever, when he stayed the pestilence. You too, then a young man, went into every sick house; many a dead body was carried out, but you came out safe — you endured many a hard trial; the helper was helped by the Helper above.
ALL. Health to the trusty man — may he long have the power to help!
FAUST. Bow before Him on high, who teaches how to help, and sends help. [He moves on with WAGNER.]

WAGNER. What a feeling, great man, you must have at the honors paid you by this multitude. Oh, happy is he who can turn his gifts to such good account. The father points you out to his boy; all ask, and press, and hurry round; the fiddle stops, the dancer pauses. As you go by, they range themselves in rows, caps fly into the air, and they all but bend the knee, as if the Host were passing.

FAUST. Only a few steps further, up to that stone yonder! Here we will rest from our walk. Here, many a time, I have sat, thoughtful and alone, and mortified myself with prayer and fasting. Rich in hope, firm in faith, I thought to wring the stoppage of that pestilence from the Lord of Heaven, with tears and sighs and wringing of hands. The applause of the multitude now sounds to me like derision. Oh! if you could read in my inmost soul how little father and son have deserved such honor! My father was a worthy, obscure man, who, honestly but in his own way, brooded with whimsical application on nature and her hallowed cycles; who, in the company of adepts, shut himself up in the dark kitchen, and fused opposites together by countless recipes. There was a Red Lion, a bold lover, married to the Lily in the tepid bath, and then both, with open flame, tortured from one bridal chamber to another. If the young Queen, with varied hues, then appeared in the glass — this was the medicine; the patients died, and no one inquired who recovered. Thus did we, with hellish electuaries, rage through these valleys and mountains far worse than the pestilence. I myself gave the poison to thousands; they wasted away, and I must now live to hear the reckless murderers praised!

WAGNER. How can you let that trouble you? Is it not enough for a good man to practice conscientiously and scrupulously the art handed down to him? If, in youth, you honor your father, you will willingly learn from him; if, in manhood, you extend the bounds of knowledge, your son may rise still higher than you.

FAUST. Oh, happy is he who can still hope to emerge from this sea of error! What we do not know is just what we need, and what we know is of no use. But let us not embitter the blessing of this hour with such melancholy reflections. See how the green-girt cottages shimmer in the setting sun! He bows and sinks — the day is done. Yonder he hurries off, and quickens other life. Oh, that I had no wing to lift me from the ground, to chase after him forever! I would see, in everlasting evening beams, the still world at my feet — every height on fire, every valley at rest, the silver brook flowing into golden streams. The rugged mountain, with all its dark defiles, would no longer break my godlike course. Already the sea, with its heated bays, opens to my enraptured sight. Yet the god seems at last to sink away. But the new impulse wakes. I hurry on to drink his everlasting light — the day before me and the night behind, the heavens above, and under me the waves. A glorious dream, but he vanishes. Alas! no bodily wing will so easily be joined to the wings of the mind. Yet it is the inborn tendency of our being that our feelings strive upward and onward; when, above us, lost in the blue expanse, the lark sings its trilling song; when, over rugged pine-covered heights, the outspread eagle soars; and over marsh and sea, the crane struggles onward to her home.

WAGNER. I myself have often had my whimsical moments, but I have never yet felt an impulse of that kind. One soon looks one's fill of woods and fields. I shall never envy the wings of the bird. How differently the pleasures of the mind bear us, from book to book, from page to page! With them, winter nights become cheerful and bright, a happy life warms every limb, and, ah, when you unroll a venerable parchment, all heaven descends to you.

FAUST. You are aware of only one impulse. Oh, never come to know the other! Two souls, alas, dwell in my breast: the one would gladly part from the other. The one, with sensuous love, clings to the world with tenacious organs; the other lifts itself energetically from the mist toward the realms of an exalted ancestry. Oh! if there are spirits in the air, hovering and ruling between earth and heaven, descend from your golden atmosphere, and lead me off to a new, varied life. Yes, if only a magic mantle were mine, and could carry me into foreign lands, I would not part with it for the costliest garments — not for a king's mantle.

WAGNER. Do not invoke that well-known troop, which streams and spreads through the atmosphere, and prepares danger in a thousand forms, from every quarter, against man. The sharp-fanged spirits, with arrowy tongues, press upon you from the north; from the east they come parching, and feed on your lungs. If the south sends from the desert those that heap fire upon fire upon your brain, the west brings the swarm which only refreshes — to drown fields, meadows, and yourself. They listen readily, ever keenly alert for mischief; they obey with pleasure, because they delight in deluding; they pretend to be sent from heaven, and lisp like angels when they lie. But let us be going; the earth is already grown grey, the air is chill, the mist is falling; it is only in the evening that we set a proper value on our homes. Why do you stand still, and gaze in astonishment like that? What can fix your attention so in the gloaming?
FAUST. Do you see the black dog ranging through the corn and stubble?
WAGNER. I saw him long ago; he did not strike me as anything particular. FAUST. Mark him well! For what do you take the brute?

WAGNER. For a poodle who, in his way, is puzzling out the track of his master. FAUST. Do you notice how, in wide spiral circles, he courses round us and ever nearer? And, if I am not mistaken, a line of fire follows on his track.
WAGNER. I see nothing but a black poodle; you may be deceived by some optical illusion.
FAUST. It seems to me that he is drawing light magical nooses, to form a snare round our feet.
WAGNER. I see him bounding hesitantly and shyly round us, because, instead of his master, he sees two strangers.
FAUST. The circle grows narrow; he is already close.
WAGNER. You see, it is a dog, and no phantom. He growls and hesitates, crouches on his belly and wags his tail — all as dogs are accustomed to do.
FAUST. Come to us! — Here!

WAGNER. He's a droll creature of a dog. Stand still, and he will sit on his hind legs; speak to him, and he will jump up on you; lose something, and he will fetch it for you, and jump into the water for your stick.
FAUST. I believe you are right; I find no trace of a spirit, and it is all training.
WAGNER. Even a wise man may grow attached to a dog when it is well brought up. Yes, he richly deserves all your favor — he, the apt pupil of the students.
[They enter the gate of the town.]

chapters.title: The Study, Part 1
paragraphs: [FAUST enters with the Poodle.] FAUST. I have left plain and meadow veiled in deep night, which wakes the better soul within us with a holy feeling of foreboding awe. Wild desires are now sunk in sleep, with every act of violence: the love of man is stirring — the love of God is stirring now. Be quiet, poodle! Don't run hither and thither. Why are you sniffing at the threshold? Lie down behind the stove; there is my best cushion for you. As outside, on the mountain path, you amused us by running and gambolling, so now accept my kindness as a welcome, quiet guest. Ah! when the friendly lamp is again burning in our narrow cell, then all becomes clear in our bosom — in the heart that knows itself. Reason begins to speak, and hope to bloom, again; we yearn for the streams, yes, for the very fountain of life. Don't growl, poodle! That brutish sound ill suits the hallowed tones which now possess my whole troubled spirit. One of us two must leave the cell. It is with reluctance that I withdraw the rights of hospitality; the door is open — the way is clear for you. But what do I see! Can that happen by natural means? Is it a shadow? Is it real? How long and broad my poodle grows! He raises himself powerfully; that is not the form of a dog! What a phantom I have brought into the house! He looks already like a hippopotamus, with fiery eyes, terrific teeth. Ah! I am sure of you! Solomon's key is good for such a half-hellish brood. SPIRITS (in the passage). One is caught within! Stay outside, follow no one. As in the snare the fox, an old lynx of hell is quaking. But take heed! Hover this way, hover back, up and down, and he is loose! If you can help him, do not leave him in the lurch, for he has already done us many a service.

FAUST. First, to confront the beast, I use the spell of the four: Salamander shall glow, Undine shall twine, ... poured through all heaven, vilely pierced through? Spellbound behind the stove, it is swelling like an elephant; it fills the whole space, it is about to vanish into mist. Don't rise to the ceiling! Down at your master's feet! You see I do not threaten in vain. I will scorch you with holy fire. Don't wait for the thrice glowing light. Don't wait for the strongest of my spells. [MEPHISTOPHELES comes forward as the mist subsides, in the dress of a Travelling Scholar, from behind the stove.]
MEPHISTOPHELES. Why such a fuss? What may be your pleasure?
FAUST. So this, then, was the kernel of the poodle! A travelling scholar? The case makes me laugh.
MEPHISTOPHELES. I salute your learned worship. You have made me sweat with a vengeance.
FAUST. What is your name?
MEPHISTOPHELES. The question strikes me as trivial for one who values the Word so little; who, far removed from all mere outward seeming, looks only to the essence of things.
FAUST. With such gentlemen as you, one can usually learn the essence from the name, since it appears only too plainly, when your name is fly-god, destroyer, liar. Now, in a word — who are you, then?
MEPHISTOPHELES. A part of that power which ever wills evil and ever produces good.

FAUST. What is meant by this riddle? MEPHISTOPHELES. I am the spirit that constantly denies! And rightly so; for everything that has come into being deserves to be annihilated. Therefore it would be better if nothing came into being. Thus, all that you call sin, destruction — in a word, Evil — is my proper element.
FAUST. You call yourself a part, and yet stand whole before me?

MEPHISTOPHELES. I tell you the modest truth. Although man, that microcosm of folly, commonly takes himself for a whole: I am a part of the part which in the beginning was all; a part of the darkness which brought forth light — the proud light, which now contests its ancient rank and space with mother Night. But it does not succeed; for, strive as it will, it clings, as if bound, to bodies. It streams from bodies, it gives beauty to bodies; a body stops it in its course, and so, I hope, it will perish along with bodies before long.

FAUST. You cannot destroy on the grand scale. MEPHISTOPHELES. And in truth, not much is accomplished that way. What stands against the Nothing — the Something, this clumsy world — for all that I have already undertaken, I have not been able to overcome. Sea and land remain undisturbed in the end. And the damned brood of beasts and men — there is no getting the better of them. How many I have already buried! And always new, fresh blood goes circulating. Out of air, water, earth — in dry, wet, warm, cold — a thousand germs unwind themselves. Had I not reserved fire to myself, I would have nothing apart for my own.
FAUST. So you oppose the cold devil's fist to the ever stirring, salutary creating power. Strange son of Chaos, try your hand at something else!
MEPHISTOPHELES. We will really think it over;
FAUST. I do not see why you ask. I have now made your acquaintance; come visit me as you please.
FAUST. Now I know your dignified calling. You are not able to destroy on a grand scale, so you do it on a small one.

MEPHISTOPHELES. And, to tell the truth, little can be achieved by this process. That which is opposed to nothingness — the Something, this clumsy world — much as I have already tried, I have not yet been able to overcome it with waves, storms, earthquakes, fire. Sea and land remain undisturbed in the end! And the damned set, the brood of beasts and men, there is no such thing as getting the better of them either. How many I have already buried! And new fresh blood is constantly circulating! Things keep going on like this — it is enough to drive one mad! From air, water, earth — in wet, dry, hot, cold — germs by the thousand evolve themselves. Had I not reserved fire to myself, I would have nothing set apart for my own.
FAUST. So you oppose your cold devil's fist, clenched in impotent malice, to the ever-stirring, beneficent creating power. Try your hand at something else, strange son of Chaos.
MEPHISTOPHELES. We will think about it in good earnest — more on that another time! Might I be permitted this time to leave?
FAUST. I do not see why you ask. I have now made your acquaintance; call on me in future as you feel inclined. Here is the window, here the door; there is also a chimney for you.
MEPHISTOPHELES. To tell the truth, a small obstacle prevents me from walking out — the wizard-foot upon your threshold.
FAUST. The Pentagram embarrasses you? Then tell me, child of hell, if that repels you, how did you come in? How was such a spirit entrapped?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Mark it well! It is not well drawn; one angle, the outward one, is, as you see, a little open.
FAUST. It is a lucky accident. So you are my prisoner now? This is a chance hit.
MEPHISTOPHELES. The poodle noticed nothing when he jumped in. The case has a different look now; the devil cannot get out.
FAUST. But why do you not go through the window?
MEPHISTOPHELES. It is a law binding on devils and phantoms that they must go out the same way they stole in. The first is free to us; we are slaves with regard to the second.
FAUST. Hell itself has its laws? I am glad of it; in that case a binding compact may be made with you gentlemen?

MEPHISTOPHELES. What is promised, that you shall enjoy to the letter; not the smallest deduction shall be made from it. But this is not to be discussed so summarily, and we will speak of it the next time. But now I most earnestly beg of you to let me go for the present.
FAUST. Wait yet a moment, and tell me some pleasant news.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Let me go now! I will soon come back; you may then question me as you like.
FAUST. I laid no snare for you; you have run into the net of your own free will. Let whoever has got hold of the devil keep hold of him. He will not catch him a second time in a hurry.
MEPHISTOPHELES. If you like, I am ready to stay and keep you company here — but on condition that I may beguile the time worthily for you with my arts.
FAUST. I shall attend with pleasure; you may do so, provided only that the art is an agreeable one.

MEPHISTOPHELES. My friend, you will gain more for your senses in this one hour than in a whole year's monotony. What the delicate spirits sing to you, the lovely images they call up, are not an insubstantial play of enchantment. Your sense of smell will be charmed, you will delight your palate, and then your feelings will be entranced. No preparation is necessary; we are all assembled — strike up! SPIRITS. Vanish, you dark arched ceilings above! Let the friendly blue sky look in more charmingly! If only the dark clouds were melted away! Little stars sparkle, softer suns shine in. The ethereal beauty of the children of heaven, tremulously bending, hovers across; longing desire follows after. And the fluttering ribbons of drapery cover the plains, cover the bower, where lovers, deep in thought, give themselves for life, bower upon bower! Sprouting tendrils! Down-weighing grapes gush into the vat of the hard-squeezing press. The foaming wines gush in brooks, rustle through pure, precious stones, leave the heights lying behind them, broaden into lakes around the charm of green-growing hills. And the winged throng sips happiness, flies to meet the sun, flies to meet the bright isles, which dancingly float on the waves; where we hear shouting in choruses, where we see dancers on meadows; all in the open air sporting alike. Some are clambering over the heights, others are swimming over the lakes, others are hovering — all toward the life, all toward the distant regions of loving stars, of blissful grace.

MEPHISTOPHELES. He slumbers! Well done, my airy, delicate youngsters! You have fairly sung him to sleep. I am your debtor for this concert. You are not yet the man to hold the devil fast! Play round him with sweet dreamy visions; plunge him into a sea of illusion. But to break the spell of this threshold I need a rat's tooth. I do not have to conjure long; one is already rustling here, and will hear me in a moment. The lord of rats and mice, of flies, frogs, bugs and lice, commands you to come forth and gnaw this threshold as soon as he has touched it with oil. You come hopping out already! Quick, to the work! The point that repelled me is toward the front on the ledge. One more bite, and it is done. Now, Faust, dream on, till we meet again.
FAUST (WAKING). Am I, then, deceived once again? Does the throng of spirits vanish like this, and has the Devil deceptively appeared to me in a dream, and has only a poodle escaped?

chapters.title: The Study, Part 2
paragraphs: FAUST — MEPHISTOPHELES.
FAUST. Is someone knocking? Come in! Who wants to disturb me again?
MEPHISTOPHELES. It is I.
FAUST. Come in.
MEPHISTOPHELES. You must say so three times. FAUST. Come in, then!

MEPHISTOPHELES. So you please me. We shall agree very well together, I hope; for, to chase away your fancies, I am here, like a gentleman of rank, in a coat of scarlet laced with gold, a mantle of stiff silk, a cock's feather in my hat, and a long pointed sword at my side. And to make no more words about it, my advice to you is to dress yourself in the same manner immediately, so that, unrestrained and free, you may try what life is.

FAUST. In every dress, I dare say, I shall feel the torture of the contracted life of this earth. I am too old just to play, too young to be without desire. What can the world give me? You shall renounce! You shall renounce! That is the eternal song which rings in everyone's ears; which, our whole life long, every hour is hoarsely singing to us. In the morning I wake only to horror. I could weep bitter tears to see the day, which, in its course, will not fulfill a wish for me, no, not one; which, with wayward captiousness, weakens even the foretaste of every joy, and disturbs the creation of my busy breast with a thousand ugly realities. Then again, when night comes, I must stretch myself in anguish on my bed; here, too, no rest is granted to me; wild dreams are sure to harrow me. The god that dwells in my bosom, who can stir my inmost soul, who sways all my energies — he is powerless as to things outside; and so existence is a burden to me, death is desired, and life hateful.
MEPHISTOPHELES. And yet death is never an entirely welcome guest.

FAUST. Oh, happy the man around whose brows he wreathes the bloody laurel in the glitter of victory — whom, after the maddening dance, he finds in a maiden's arms. Oh, that I had sunk away, enraptured, lifeless, before the great spirit's power!
MEPHISTOPHELES. And yet a certain person did not drink a certain brown juice on a certain night.
FAUST. Spying, it seems, is your amusement.
MEPHISTOPHELES. I am not omniscient; but much is known to me.

FAUST. If a sweet familiar tone drew me from that terrible tumult, and beguiled the remnants of my childlike feelings with the echo of a happier time, I now curse everything that entwines the soul with false alluring jugglery, and spellbinds it in this den of wretchedness with dazzling and flattering influences. Cursed, first, be the lofty opinion in which the mind wraps itself! Cursed, the dazzling of appearances, by which our senses are subdued! Cursed, the hypocrite dreams — the delusion of glory and of an everlasting name! Cursed, what flatters us as property, as wife and child, as slave and plough! Cursed be Mammon when he stirs us to bold deeds with treasures, when he smooths our couch for indolent delight! My curse on the balsam-juice of the grape! My curse on that highest favor of love! My curse on Hope, my curse on Faith, and my curse, above all, on Patience! CHORUS OF SPIRITS (invisible). Woe, woe, you have destroyed it, the beautiful world, with violent hand; it falls, it is broken! A demigod has shattered it to pieces! We bear away the wrecks into nothingness, and wail over the beauty that is lost. Mighty one among the sons of earth, build it more proudly again, build it up in your bosom! Begin a new course of life, with unclouded sense, and new songs shall peal out upon it.

MEPHISTOPHELES. These are the little ones of my train. Listen — with wisdom beyond their years, they counsel you to pleasure and action. They would gladly lure you out into the world, away from solitariness, where senses and the sap of life stagnate. Stop trifling with your grief, which, like a vulture, feeds upon your vitals. The worst company will make you feel that you are a man among men. Yet I do not mean to thrust you into the common throng. I am not one of the great ones; but if, united with me, you will make your way through life, I will readily make myself yours on the spot. I am your companion; and, if you are satisfied, I am your servant, your slave!
FAUST. And what am I to do for you in return?
MEPHISTOPHELES. For that you still have a long day of grace.
FAUST. No, no; the devil is an egoist, and is not likely to do for nothing what is useful to another. State the condition plainly; such a servant is a dangerous inmate.
MEPHISTOPHELES. I will bind myself to your service here, and never rest or repose at your call. When we meet on the other side, you shall do as much for me.

FAUST. I care little about the other side: if you first knock this world to pieces, the other may arise afterwards as it pleases. My joys flow from this earth, and this sun shines upon my sufferings; if I can only separate myself from them, whatever will and can happen, may then come to pass. I will hear no more about it — whether there is hating and loving in the world to come, and whether there is an Above or Below in those spheres too.
MEPHISTOPHELES. In this mood, you may venture it. Bind yourself; and during these days, you shall be delighted by my arts; I will give you what no human being has ever yet seen.

FAUST. What, poor devil, will you give? Was a man's mind, in its high aspiring, ever understood by the likes of you? But do you have food that does not satisfy? Red gold which, volatile as quicksilver, melts away in the hand? A game at which one never wins? A maiden who, on my breast, is already ogling my neighbor? The bright godlike joy of honor, which vanishes like a meteor? Show me the fruit that rots before it is plucked, and trees that grow green anew every day.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Such a task does not frighten me. I have such treasures at my disposal. But, my good friend, the time will come round when we would like to feast on what is really good in peace.

FAUST. If ever I stretch myself composed on a bed of indolence, let that be the end of me. If you can ever flatteringly delude me into being pleased with myself — if you can cheat me with enjoyment, let that day be my last. I offer the wager. MEPHISTOPHELES. Done!

FAUST. Done! And my hand upon it! If I ever say to the passing moment — Stay, you are so fair! then you may cast me into chains; then I will gladly perish! Then may the death-bell toll; then are you free from your service, the clock may stand, the hand may fall, and time be no more for me!

MEPHISTOPHELES. Think it over well! We shall not forget it. FAUST. You have a perfect right to that; I have not rashly overreached myself. As I persist, so am I a slave — whether yours, what do I ask, or anyone's.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Today, at the doctor's feast, I shall enter on my duty. Only one thing — for life or death's sake, I beg of you a line or two.

FAUST. Pedant, do you, too, require something written? Have you never known a man or a man's word? Is it not enough that my spoken word should govern my days forever? And shall a promise hold me? Yet this delusion is implanted in our hearts: who would willingly free himself from it? Happy the man who bears truth pure in his breast; no sacrifice will ever cause him regret! But a parchment, written and stamped, is a spectre from which all shrink. The word dies away in the very pen; in wax and leather lies the mastery. What, evil spirit, would you have of me? Brass, marble, parchment, paper? Shall I write with stylus, chisel, pen? I leave the choice to you. MEPHISTOPHELES. How can you so passionately declaim and exaggerate?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Consider it well! We shall keep it in mind.
FAUST. You have a perfect right to do so. I have formed no rash estimate of myself. As I drag on, I am a slave; what does it matter to me, whether yours or another's?
MEPHISTOPHELES. This very day, at the doctor's feast, I shall enter upon my duty as servant. Only one thing — to guard against accidents, I must trouble you for a line or two.

FAUST. Pedant, do you, too, require writing? Have you never known a man, or a man's word? Is it not enough that my word of mouth disposes of my days for all eternity? Does not the world rave on in all its currents, and am I to be bound by a promise? Yet this prejudice is implanted in our hearts: who would willingly free himself from it? Happy the man who bears truth pure in his breast; he will never have cause to regret any sacrifice! But a parchment, written and stamped, is a spectre that all shrink from. The word dies away in the very pen; in wax and leather is the mastery. What, evil spirit, would you have of me? Brass, marble, parchment, paper? Shall I write with stylus, graver, pen? I leave the choice to you. MEPHISTOPHELES. How can you so passionately declaim and exaggerate? Any scrap will do. You will sign your name with a drop of blood.
FAUST. If this will fully satisfy you, let the whim be indulged.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Blood is quite a peculiar sort of juice.

FAUST. Only no fear that I shall break this compact. What I promise is precisely what all my energies strive for. I have aspired too high: I belong only to your class. The Great Spirit has spurned me; Nature shuts herself against me. The thread of thought is snapped; I have long loathed every sort of knowledge. Let us quench our glowing passions in the depths of sensuality! Let every wonder be forthwith prepared beneath the hitherto impenetrable veil of sorcery. Let us cast ourselves into the rushing of time, into the rolling of events. There pain and pleasure, success and disappointment, may follow each other as they will — in restless activity alone is a man proved.

MEPHISTOPHELES. No end nor limit is prescribed to you. If it is your pleasure to sip the sweets of everything, to snatch at all as you fly by, much good may it do you — only fall to, and don't be coy.

FAUST. I tell you again, pleasure is not the question: I devote myself to the intoxicating whirl — to the most agonizing enjoyment — to enamored hate — to invigorating vexation. My breast, cured of the thirst for knowledge, shall henceforth bare itself to every pang. I will enjoy, in my own heart's core, all that is parcelled out among mankind; grasp in spirit the highest and the deepest; heap the weal and woe of the whole race upon my breast, and so expand my own self to theirs, and perish also, in the end, like them.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Oh, believe me, who for many thousand years have chewed this hard food, that, from cradle to grave, no human being digests the old leaven. Believe a being like me, this Whole is made only for a god. He exists in an eternal halo; us he has brought forth into darkness, and only day and night are proper for you.
FAUST. But I will.

MEPHISTOPHELES. There is some sense in that! But I am only troubled about one thing; time is short, art is long. I think you should let yourself be advised. Take a poet to counsel; make the gentleman set his imagination to work, and heap all noble qualities on your honored head — the lion's courage, the stag's swiftness, the fiery blood of the Italian, the endurance of the North. Make him find out the secret of combining magnanimity with cunning, and of being in love, according to a set plan, with the burning desires of youth. I myself should like to know such a gentleman — I would call him Mr. Microcosm.
FAUST. What, then, am I, if it is not possible to attain the crown of humanity, which every sense is striving for?
MEPHISTOPHELES. You are in the end — what you are. Put on wigs with a million curls — set your foot upon ell-high heels — you remain what you are.

FAUST. I feel it; in vain have I scraped together and accumulated all the treasures of the human mind upon myself; and when I sit down at the end, still no new power wells up within me: I am not a hair's breadth higher, not a whit nearer the Infinite.

MEPHISTOPHELES. My good sir, you see things precisely as they are ordinarily seen; we must manage matters better before the joys of life pass from us. What the deuce! you have surely hands and feet, and head and backside; and what I enjoy with spirit, is that any less my own? If I can pay for six horses, are not their powers mine? I dash along and am a proper man, as if I had four-and-twenty legs. Quick, then, have done with poring, and straight away into the world with me. I tell you, a fellow who speculates is like a brute driven in a circle on a barren heath by an evil spirit, while fair green meadow lies everywhere around.
FAUST. How shall we set about it?

MEPHISTOPHELES. We will just start and take our chances. What a place of martyrdom this is! What a precious life to lead — wearying oneself and a set of youngsters to death! Leave that to your neighbor, Mr. Paunch! Why will you plague yourself thrashing straw? The best you can know, you dare not tell the lads. Even now I hear one in the passage.
FAUST. I cannot possibly see him.
MEPHISTOPHELES. The poor boy has waited long; he must not be sent away disconsolate. Come, give me your cap and gown; the mask will become me admirably.
[He changes his dress.]
Now trust to my wit. I require only a quarter of an hour. In the meantime prepare for our pleasant trip. [Exit FAUST.]

MEPHISTOPHELES (IN FAUST'S GOWN). Only despise reason and knowledge, the highest strength of humanity; only let yourself be confirmed in delusion and sorcery by the spirit of lies — and I have you unconditionally. Fate has given him a spirit that is ever pressing onward, uncurbed, and whose overstrained striving overleaps the joys of earth. I will drag him through the wild passages of life, through vapid insignificance. He shall sprawl, stand amazed, stick fast — and meat and drink shall hang, for his insatiable appetite, before his craving lips; he shall pray for refreshment in vain, and even had he not already given himself to the devil, he would, nevertheless, inevitably be lost. [A STUDENT enters.]
STUDENT. I have only just arrived, and come, full of devotion, to pay my respects to, and make the acquaintance of, a man whom everyone names to me with reverence.
MEPHISTOPHELES. I am flattered by your politeness. You see a man, like many others. Have you yet made any inquiry elsewhere?

STUDENT. Take an interest in me, I beg you. I come with every good disposition, a little money, and youthful spirits; my mother could hardly be brought to part with me, but I want to learn something worth learning in the world.

MEPHISTOPHELES. You are here at the very place for it. STUDENT. Honestly speaking, I already wish myself away: these walls, these halls, are by no means to my taste. The space is extremely confined; there is not a tree, nothing green, to be seen; and in the lecture rooms, on the benches, hearing, sight, and thinking fail me.

MEPHISTOPHELES. It all depends on habit. So, at first, the child does not take kindly to the mother's breast, but soon finds pleasure in nourishing itself. Just so, you will daily experience a greater pleasure at the breasts of wisdom.
STUDENT. I shall hang delightedly upon her neck; only tell me how I am to attain it.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Tell me, before you go further, what faculty you fix upon?
STUDENT. I should wish to be profoundly learned, and would like to comprehend everything that is upon earth or in heaven — all science and nature.
MEPHISTOPHELES. You are here on the right track; but you must not let your attention be distracted.
STUDENT. I am heart and soul in the cause; but a little relaxation and pastime, to be sure, would not come amiss on bright summer holidays.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Make the most of time, it glides away so fast; still, method will teach you to gain time. For this reason, my good friend, I advise you to begin with a course of logic. In this study, the mind is well broken in — laced up in Spanish boots, so that it may creep circumspectly along the path of thought, and runs no risk of flickering, like a will-o'-the-wisp, in all directions. Then many a day will be spent in teaching you that one, two, three is necessary for what formerly you hit off at a blow, as easily as eating and drinking. It is true, the factory of thought is like a weaver's masterpiece, where one treadle moves a thousand threads; the shuttles shoot back and forth, the threads flow unseen; ties, by the thousand, are struck off at a blow: your philosopher steps in and proves to you that this must needs be so: the first is so, the second so, and therefore the third and fourth are so; and if the first and second were not, the third and fourth would never be. The students of all countries put a high value on this, but none have become weavers. Whoever wishes to know and describe anything living, seeks first to drive the spirit out of it; he then has the parts in his hand — only, alas, the spiritual bond is missing. Chemistry calls it encheiresis naturae, and mocks itself without knowing it.
STUDENT. I cannot quite understand you.

MEPHISTOPHELES. You will soon improve in that respect, if you learn to reduce and classify all things properly. STUDENT. I am so confounded by all this, I feel as if a millwheel were turning round in my head.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Next, before everything else, you must set to at metaphysics. There, take care to grasp profoundly what is not made for human brains. A fine word will stand you in good stead for what enters and what does not enter there. And be sure, for this half-year, to adopt the strictest regularity. You will have five lectures every day. Be in as the clock strikes. Be well prepared beforehand, with the paragraphs carefully conned, that you may see the better that he says nothing but what is in the book; and write away as zealously as if the Holy Ghost were dictating to you.
STUDENT. You need not tell me that a second time. I can imagine how useful it is. For what one has in black and white, one can carry home in comfort.
MEPHISTOPHELES. But choose a faculty.
STUDENT. I cannot reconcile myself to jurisprudence.

MEPHISTOPHELES. I cannot much blame you. I know the nature of this science. Laws descend, like an inveterate hereditary disease; they trail from generation to generation, and glide imperceptibly from place to place. Reason becomes nonsense; beneficence, calamity. Woe to you that you are a grandson! Of the law that is born with us — of that, unfortunately, there is never a question.
STUDENT. You increase my repugnance. Oh, happy he whom you instruct. I should almost like to study theology.

MEPHISTOPHELES. I do not wish to mislead you. As for this science, it is so difficult to avoid the wrong way; there is so much hidden poison in it, which is hardly to be distinguished from the medicine. Here, again, it is best to attend only one master, and swear by his words. On the whole, stick to words; you will then pass through the safe gate into the temple of certainty.
STUDENT. But there must be some meaning connected with the word.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Right! Only we must not be too anxious about that; for it is precisely where ideas fail that a word comes in most opportunely. With words one can argue admirably; with words one can form a system; it is easy to believe in words; from a word not an iota can be taken.

STUDENT. Your pardon, I detain you with my many questions, but I must trouble you still. Would you be so kind as to add a pregnant word or two on medicine? Three years is a short time, and the field, God knows, is far too wide. If one has but a hint, one can feel one's way along further.

MEPHISTOPHELES (ASIDE). I begin to be tired of the prosing style. I must play the genuine devil again. [Aloud.] The spirit of medicine is easy to grasp; you study through the great and little world, and let things go on in the end — as it pleases God. It is in vain that you wander scientifically about; no man will learn more than he can; he who avails himself of the passing moment — that is the proper man. You are tolerably well built, nor will you be wanting in boldness, and if you only have confidence in yourself, other souls will trust you. In particular, learn how to treat the women: their eternal ohs and ahs, so thousand-fold, are all to be cured from a single point, and if you only assume a moderately demure air, you will have them all under your thumb. You must have a title to convince them that your art is superior to most others, and then you are admitted from the first to all those little privileges for which another has to coax many a year. Learn how to press the pulse adroitly, and boldly clasp them, with sly fiery glances, around the tapering hip, to see how tightly it is laced.
STUDENT. There is some sense in that; at any rate one sees the where and the how.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Grey, my dear friend, is all theory, and green the golden tree of life.
STUDENT. I vow to you, it seems like a dream to me. Might I trouble you another time to hear your wisdom fully expounded?
MEPHISTOPHELES. I am at your service, to the extent of my poor abilities. STUDENT. I cannot possibly go away without putting my album in your hands. Do not grudge me this token of your favor.
MEPHISTOPHELES. With all my heart. [He writes and gives it back.]
STUDENT (READS). Eritis sicut Deus, scientes bonum et malum. [He closes the book reverentially, and takes his leave.]
MEPHISTOPHELES. Only follow the old saying, and my cousin the snake, and your resemblance to God will surely cause you anxiety one day.
FAUST (ENTERS). Where now?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Where you please; to see the little, then the great, world. With what joy, what profit, will you revel through the course!

FAUST. But with my long beard, I lack the easy manners of society. I shall fail in the attempt. I never knew how to present myself in the world, I feel so small in the presence of others; I shall be in a constant state of embarrassment.
MEPHISTOPHELES. My dear friend, all that will come of its own accord; as soon as you feel confidence in yourself, you know the art of life.
FAUST. How, then, are we to start? Where are your carriages, horses, and servants?

MEPHISTOPHELES. We have only to spread out this mantle; that shall bear us through the air. Only you will take no heavy baggage on this bold trip. A little inflammable air, which I will get ready, will lift us quickly from this earth; and if we are light, we shall mount rapidly. I wish you joy of your new course of life. [Carousal of merry fellows.]
FROSCH. Will no one drink? No one laugh? I'll teach you to make faces! Today you are like wet straw, when usually you blaze in full flame.
BRANDER. The fault is yours; you bring nothing along — not one bit of nonsense, not one piece of mischief. Here, take that — both!
BRANDER. Double swine!
FROSCH. You wanted it — that's what you are!
SIEBEL. With open chest, sing the round, swill and shout! Up! Holla! Ho!
ALTMAYER. Woe is me, I am lost! Bring cotton! The fellow is splitting my ears.

chapters.title: Auerbach's Cellar in Leipzig
paragraphs: [A drinking bout of merry fellows.]
FROSCH. Nobody drinking? Nobody laughing? None of your gloomy faces here! You’re all like wet straw today, but at other times you blaze brightly enough.
BRANDER. That’s your own fault — you’re contributing nothing yourself: no nonsense, no obscenity.
FROSCH (throws a glass of wine over BRANDER’s head). There — you’ve got both!
BRANDER. You double swine!
FROSCH. Well — you wanted me to be one.
SIEBEL. Throw out anyone who quarrels! Open your throats and strike up a chorus! Swill and shout — holla, holla, ho!
ALTMAYER. Woe is me — I’m a lost man! Cotton, here, quickly! The fellow’s splitting my ears.
SIEBEL. It’s only when the vault echoes back that you really feel the power of the bass.
FROSCH. Right — and throw out anyone who takes it the wrong way. Ah! Tra la la!
ALTMAYER. Tra la la!
FROSCH. Our throats are tuned. [He sings.] “The dear old Holy Roman Empire — what is it that holds it together still?”

BRANDER. A nasty song! Bah, a political song! An offensive song! Thank God every morning of your life that you don’t have the Roman Empire to worry about! I, at any rate, count it no small advantage that I’m neither emperor nor chancellor. But we can’t do without a head — so let’s elect ourselves a pope. You know what kind of qualification tips the scales and lifts the man up.
FROSCH (sings). “Soar up, Dame Nightingale — give my sweetheart a thousand greetings from me.”
SIEBEL. No greeting to the sweetheart! I won’t hear of it!
FROSCH. A greeting to the sweetheart — and a kiss too! You won’t stop me. [He sings.] Open the bolts, in the still of night. Open the bolts — the lover’s awake. Shut the bolts, at the break of day.

SIEBEL. Yes, sing on, sing and praise and celebrate her — my time for laughing will come. She’s taken me in; she’ll do the same to you. May she find herself a hobgoblin for a lover! Let him toy with her at the crossroads. May an old he-goat, returning from the Brocken, bleat her a goodnight at the gallop. A proper fellow of real flesh and blood is far too good for that wench. I won’t hear of a greeting — unless it’s to smash her windows. BRANDER (striking on the table). Attention, attention! Listen to me! You gentlemen must allow that I know something of life. There are lovesick people here, and I must give them something suitable to their condition by way of goodnight. Listen! A song in the newest style — and strike in boldly with the chorus.
[He sings.]

“There was once a rat in the cellar, who lived on nothing but fat and butter, and had grown himself a paunch like Doctor Luther. The cook laid poison out for him; then the world got too hot for him — as though he had love in his body.” CHORUS. As though he had love in his body.

BRANDER. “He ran round, he ran out, he drank from every puddle, he gnawed and scratched at the whole house, but his fury did him no good. He made many a leap of agony — the poor beast was soon finished, as though he had love in his body.”
CHORUS. As though he had love in his body.

BRANDER. “He came running into the kitchen in sheer pain, in broad daylight, fell on the hearth and lay convulsed, panting pitifully. Then the poisoner cried out with a laugh — Ha, he’s at his last gasp! As though he had love in his body.”

CHORUS. As though he had love in his body. SIEBEL. How the flats chuckle! It’s a fine thing, to be sure — laying poison for the poor rats. BRANDER. Perhaps they stand high in your favour? ALTMAYER.
