The bald-pated pot-belly! Misfortune makes him humble and mild. He sees in the swollen rat his own portrait, drawn to the life. FAUST and MEPHISTOPHELES enter.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Above all else, I must introduce you to merry company, so you may see how lightly life can be passed. For these people every day is a feast. With a little wit and a lot of self-satisfaction, each one spins around in his narrow circle-dance, like kittens playing with their tails. So long as they’ve no headache to complain of, and so long as they can get credit from the landlord, they’re merry and free from care.
BRANDER. They’re just back from a journey — you can see it in their strange manner. They haven’t been here an hour.
FROSCH. You’re right! Leipzig is the place for me! It’s a little Paris, and it gives its people a polish.
SIEBEL. What do you take the strangers to be?
FROSCH. Leave it to me! Over a good glass I’ll worm it out of them as easily as drawing a child’s tooth. They look noble to me — they have a proud, discontented air.
BRANDER. Mountebanks, I’ll wager — for certain.
ALTMAYER. Perhaps.
FROSCH. Now watch — I’ll smoke them out.
MEPHISTOPHELES (to Faust). These folk would never scent the devil, even if he had them by the throat.
FAUST. Our greetings, gentlemen.
SIEBEL. Many thanks to you in return. [Aside, looking askance at MEPHISTOPHELES.] What? Does the fellow limp on one foot?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Will you allow us to sit down with you? We’ll have your company to cheer us, instead of good liquor, which isn’t to be had.
ALTMAYER. You seem a very particular gentleman.
FROSCH. You probably left Rippach at a late hour? Did you sup with Mr. Hans before you went?

MEPHISTOPHELES. We passed him without stopping today. The last time, though, we spoke with him. He had much to say about his cousins, and charged us with many greetings to each of them. [With a bow toward Frosch.]
ALTMAYER (aside). There — he has you! He knows a thing or two! SIEBEL. A knowing fellow!
FROSCH. Just wait — I’ll have him in a moment.
MEPHISTOPHELES. If I’m not mistaken, we heard some practised voices singing in chorus? Singing must echo splendidly from this vaulted roof. FROSCH. Are you perhaps a virtuoso?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Oh, no! The power is weak, but the desire is strong.
ALTMAYER. Give us a song.
MEPHISTOPHELES. As many as you like.
SIEBEL. Just let it be brand new. MEPHISTOPHELES. We’ve just come back from Spain, the lovely land of wine and song. [He sings.] There once was a king who had a great flea —
FROSCH. Listen! A flea! Did you catch that? A flea is a fine sort of fellow.

MEPHISTOPHELES (sings). “There once was a king, and he had a great flea, and was as fond of it as if it had been his own son. He called his tailor; the tailor came. ‘There, measure the lad for some clothes, and measure him for some breeches.’”
BRANDER. Only don’t forget to impress on the tailor that he must measure with the greatest care — and, as he loves his head, make sure the breeches fit smoothly.

MEPHISTOPHELES. “Now he was attired in velvet and silk, with ribbons on his coat and a cross besides, and was promptly made minister, and had a great star. Then his brothers also became great lords at court. And the lords and ladies at court were dreadfully tormented — from the queen to the chambermaid they were pricked and bitten, and yet they daren’t crack the fleas or scratch them away. But we crack and stifle them fast enough when one of them pricks us.”
CHORUS. But we crack and stifle them fast enough when one of them pricks us.
FROSCH. Bravo! Bravo! That was first-rate!
SIEBEL. So perish every flea!
BRANDER. Point your fingers and nip them smartly.
ALTMAYER. Liberty for ever! Wine for ever!
MEPHISTOPHELES. I’d gladly drink a glass in honour of liberty — if only your wine were a shade better.
SIEBEL. You’d better not let us hear that again!
MEPHISTOPHELES. I’m afraid the landlord would feel hurt — otherwise I’d treat these worthy gentlemen to some of our own cellar.
SIEBEL. Out with it — I take the blame on myself.

FROSCH. If you give us a good glass, we won’t be sparing of our praise. Only don’t let your samples be too small. If I’m to give my opinion, I need a proper mouthful. ALTMAYER (aside). They’re from the Rhine, I guess.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Bring me a gimlet.
BRANDER. What for? Surely you don’t have the casks at the door?
ALTMAYER. Over there is the landlord’s tool-chest.
MEPHISTOPHELES (taking the gimlet, to Frosch). Now say — what wine would you like to taste?
FROSCH. What do you mean? Have you so many kinds?
MEPHISTOPHELES. I give every man his choice.
ALTMAYER (to Frosch). Ha! You’re already licking your lips.

FROSCH. Well — if I’m to choose, I’ll take Rhine wine. Our fatherland gives the very best of gifts. MEPHISTOPHELES (boring a hole in the edge of the table where FROSCH is sitting). Get a little wax to make stoppers, right away.
ALTMAYER. Ah, these are jugglers’ tricks.
MEPHISTOPHELES (to Brander). And you?

BRANDER. I choose champagne — and let it be properly sparkling. [MEPHISTOPHELES bores; meanwhile one of the others has prepared the wax stoppers and plugged the holes.] One can’t always avoid what is foreign — what is good often lies far off. A true German can’t stand the French, but he gladly drinks their wines.
SIEBEL (as MEPHISTOPHELES approaches him). I must admit I don’t like sour wine. Give me a glass of the genuinely sweet.
MEPHISTOPHELES (bores). You shall have Tokay in a twinkling.
ALTMAYER. No, gentlemen — look me in the face. I can see plainly you’re only making fun of us.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Ha, ha! That would be taking too great a liberty with such distinguished guests. Quick now — just speak out. What wine may I have the pleasure of serving you?
ALTMAYER. Any! Only don’t waste time in asking.
[After all the holes are bored and stopped.]

MEPHISTOPHELES (with strange gestures). The vine bears grapes. The he-goat bears horns. Wine is juice; vines are wood; the wooden table can also give wine. A deep look into nature! Here’s a miracle — only have faith! Now draw the stoppers and drink. ALL (as they draw the stoppers, and the wine each has chosen runs into his glass). Oh, beautiful spring, that flows for us!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Only take care not to spill any. [They drink repeatedly.]
ALL (sing). We feel as splendidly jolly as five hundred swine.
MEPHISTOPHELES. These people are free — see how happy they are!
FAUST. I’d like to be off now.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Wait a moment — their brutishness will reveal itself gloriously. SIEBEL (drinks carelessly; the wine spills onto the ground and turns to flame). Help, fire! Help — hell is burning!
MEPHISTOPHELES (conjuring the flame). Be quiet, friendly element. (To Siebel.) This time it was only a drop of the fire of purgatory.
SIEBEL. What’s the meaning of that? Wait — you’ll pay dearly for it! It seems you don’t know who we are.
FROSCH. You’d better not try that a second time.
ALTMAYER. I think we’d better send him packing — quietly.
SIEBEL. What, sir — do you dare play your hocus-pocus here?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Silence, you old wine-cask!
SIEBEL. Broomstick! Will you even be rude to us?
BRANDER. Just wait — it shall rain blows! ALTMAYER (draws a stopper from the table; fire flies out at him). I burn! I burn!
SIEBEL. Sorcery! Strike home! The fellow’s outlawed. [They draw their knives and fall on MEPHISTOPHELES.]
MEPHISTOPHELES (with solemn gestures). False form and word, change sense and place. Be here — be there!
[They stand amazed and stare at one another.]
ALTMAYER. Where am I? What a beautiful country!
FROSCH. Vineyards! Can I believe my eyes?
SIEBEL. And grapes within reach!
BRANDER. Here, under these green leaves — look, what a stem! What a bunch! [He seizes SIEBEL by the nose. The others do the same to each other and raise their knives.]
MEPHISTOPHELES (as before). Error, loose the bandage from their eyes! And remember the devil’s way of jesting! [He disappears with Faust. The fellows start back from one another.]
SIEBEL. What’s the matter?
ALTMAYER. How?
FROSCH. Was that your nose?
BRANDER (to Siebel). And I have yours in my hand!
ALTMAYER. It was a shock that ran through every limb! Give me a chair — I’m sinking.
FROSCH. No, just tell me — what happened?

SIEBEL. Where’s the fellow? If I run into him, it’ll cost him his life. ALTMAYER. I myself saw him at the cellar door, riding out on a cask. My feet feel as heavy as lead. [Turning toward the table.] My — I wonder if the wine is still running?
SIEBEL. It was all a cheat, a lie, and a delusion.
FROSCH. Yet it seemed to me as if I were drinking wine.
BRANDER. But what about the grapes?
ALTMAYER. After that, let anyone tell me that a man shouldn’t believe in miracles!

chapters.title: Witch's Kitchen
paragraphs: A large cauldron is hanging over the fire on a low hearth. Different figures can be seen in the fumes that rise from it. A female monkey sits by the cauldron, skimming it and making sure it doesn’t boil over. The male monkey is seated nearby with the young ones, warming himself. The walls and ceiling are hung with the strangest pieces of witch-furniture.

FAUST. I loathe this mad business of witchcraft. Do you promise me I’ll recover in this chaos of insanity? Do I really need an old hag’s advice? And will this foul mess perhaps take thirty years off my life? Woe to me, if you know of nothing better! All hope is already gone. Has nature, has a noble spirit, discovered no kind of remedy?
MEPHISTOPHELES. My friend, now you’re speaking wisely again! There is a natural way of renewing youth — but it’s in another book, and it forms a very strange chapter.
FAUST. Tell me what it is.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Well — there’s a remedy to be had without money, physician, or sorcery. Take yourself straight out to the field, start to hoe and dig, keep yourself and your senses inside a sharply restricted circle, live on simple food, live with beasts as a beast, and don’t think it shameful to manure with your own hands the field from which you reap. That, believe me, is the best way to keep yourself young until eighty. FAUST. I’m not used to it. I can’t bring myself to take up a spade — that confined life doesn’t suit me at all.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Then you’ll have to fall back on the witch after all.
FAUST. But why must it be the hag? Can’t you brew the drink yourself?

MEPHISTOPHELES. That would be a fine pastime! I’d rather build a thousand bridges in the time. It takes more than art and science for this job — it takes patience. A quiet spirit works at it for years; only time strengthens this fine fermentation. And the ingredients are extraordinarily strange. The devil, true, has taught her how — but the devil can’t make it himself. [Noticing the monkeys.] Look at the pretty breed! This is the maid — that’s the man. (To the monkeys.) It seems your mistress isn’t at home? THE MONKEYS. At the feast — out of the house — out by the chimney. MEPHISTOPHELES. How long does she usually roam about? THE MONKEYS. As long as we warm our paws.
MEPHISTOPHELES (to Faust). How do you like these tender creatures?
FAUST. As disgusting as anything I’ve ever seen.
MEPHISTOPHELES. No — talk like this is exactly what I most enjoy. (To the monkeys.) Tell me, you cursed puppets — why are you stirring this mess? THE MONKEYS. We’re cooking watery soups for beggars.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Then you’ll have plenty of customers. THE HE-MONKEY (approaches and fawns on MEPHISTOPHELES). Oh, quickly throw the dice — make me rich and let me win! My fate is a sorry one, and if I had money I’d have sense as well.

MEPHISTOPHELES. [The young monkeys have been playing with a great globe and roll it forward.] THE HE-MONKEY. That is the world: it rings like glass — how soon does that break? It is hollow inside. Here it glitters much, and here still more. I am alive! My dear son — keep away from it. You must die! It is of clay — it makes potsherds.
MEPHISTOPHELES. What’s the sieve for? THE HE-MONKEY (takes it down). If you were a thief, I’d know you at once. Look through the sieve! Do you recognise the thief — and dare not name him?

MEPHISTOPHELES. How happy the monkey would think himself, if he could only play the lottery! [The young monkeys, meanwhile, have been playing with a large globe, and roll it forward.] THE HE-MONKEY. That is the world: it rises and falls, and rolls unceasingly. It rings like glass — how soon does that break? It’s hollow inside. It glitters much here, and still more here — I am alive! My dear son, keep away from it! You must die. It is of clay — this makes potsherds.

MEPHISTOPHELES. What is the sieve for? THE HE-MONKEY (takes it down). If you were a thief, I’d know you at once. [He runs to the female and makes her look through it.] Look through the sieve! Do you recognise the thief — and dare not name him?

MEPHISTOPHELES. Uncivil beast! THE HE-MONKEY. Take the brush here, and sit down on the settle. [He makes MEPHISTOPHELES sit down.] FAUST (who has been standing before a looking-glass all this time, now approaching it and now stepping back). What do I see? What a heavenly image shows itself in this magic mirror! O Love, lend me the swiftest of your wings and bear me to her region! Ah — if I don’t stay rooted to this spot, if I dare to step nearer, I can only see her as if through a mist. Must I see in those reclining limbs the very essence of all heavens? Is such a thing to be found on earth?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Naturally — when a god labours hard for six days, and at the end says “Bravo” to himself, something clever is bound to come of it.
MEPHISTOPHELES (approaching the fire). And this pot? THE MONKEYS. The half-witted sot! He doesn’t know the pot! He doesn’t know the kettle!

MEPHISTOPHELES. Uncivil brute! THE HE-MONKEY. Take the brush here, and sit down on the settle. [He makes MEPHISTOPHELES sit down. FAUST, who has been standing all this time before a looking-glass, now approaching and now stepping back.] FAUST. What do I see? What a heavenly image shows itself in this magic mirror! O Love, lend me the swiftest of your wings and bear me to her region! Ah — if I don’t stay rooted to this spot, if I dare to step nearer, I can only see her as if through a mist. The loveliest image of a woman! Is it possible — can a woman be so lovely? Must I see in these reclining limbs the very essence of all heavens? Is such a thing to be found on earth?

MEPHISTOPHELES. When a god labours for six days and himself says “Bravo” at the end, it’s only natural that something clever should come of it. For this once, look your fill. I know where to find such a love for you — and happy is the man whose luck it is to take her home as bridegroom. [Faust keeps looking into the mirror. MEPHISTOPHELES, stretching himself on the settle and playing with the brush, continues speaking.] Here I sit like a king on his throne — here is my sceptre; I only need the crown. THE MONKEYS (who have been playing all sorts of strange antics, bring MEPHISTOPHELES a crown with loud cries). Oh, be so kind as to glue the crown together with sweat and blood. [They handle the crown awkwardly and break it into two pieces, jumping about with them.] Now it’s done — we speak, and we see; we hear and we rhyme —
FAUST (before the mirror). Woe is me! I’m almost going mad!
MEPHISTOPHELES (pointing to the monkeys). Now my own head is beginning to spin. THE MONKEYS. And if we’re lucky, and if things click, then they are thoughts!
FAUST (as before). My breast is starting to burn! Do let us be off at once!

MEPHISTOPHELES (in the same position). Well, no one can deny that they’re sincere poets. [The cauldron, which the she-monkey has neglected, begins to boil over; a great flame rises and streams up the chimney. THE WITCH comes shooting down through the flame with terrible cries.]
THE WITCH. Ough, ough, ough, ough! Damned beast! Accursed sow! Neglecting the cauldron, scorching your dame — cursed beast!
[Spying Faust and MEPHISTOPHELES.]

What now? Who are you? What do you want here? Who has come slinking in? May the plague of fire get into your bones! [She dips the skimming ladle into the cauldron and sprinkles flames at Faust, MEPHISTOPHELES, and the monkeys. The monkeys whimper.] MEPHISTOPHELES (who inverts the brush in his hand and strikes among the glasses and pots). To pieces! To pieces! There lies the porridge! There lies the glass! It’s only a joke, you carrion — beating time to your melody!

MEPHISTOPHELES. For it’s been a while, after all, since we last saw each other. The march of civilisation, which licks all the world into shape, has even reached the devil. The northern phantom is no longer to be seen. And as for the foot I can’t do without — like many a young man, I’ve worn false calves for years now.
[As the witch steps back in rage and horror.]

Don’t you know me, you skeleton, you abomination? Don’t you know your lord and master? What’s to stop me striking in earnest — dashing you and your monkey-spirits to pieces? Have you no respect for the red doublet any more? Can’t you recognise the cock’s feather? Have I hidden this face? Must I name myself?
THE WITCH. Oh, master — forgive this rough reception! But I see no cloven foot. Where then are your two ravens?

MEPHISTOPHELES. This time you’ll come off unhurt — for it’s been a while, after all, since we saw each other. The march of civilisation, which licks all the world into shape, has even reached the devil. The northern phantom is no longer to be seen. Where do you see horns, tail, or claws? And as for the foot, which I can’t do without — it would tell against me in society. So, like many a young man, I’ve worn false calves these many years.
THE WITCH (dancing). I’m almost beside myself to see Squire Satan here again!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Woman — I won’t hear that name.
THE WITCH. Why? What has it done to you?

MEPHISTOPHELES. It’s long since been relegated to the book of fables — but people are no better off for that. They’re rid of the Evil One, but the evil ones have stayed behind. You may call me Lord Baron — that will do well enough. I’m a gentleman, like other gentlemen. You don’t doubt my noble blood. See — this is the coat of arms I bear! [He makes an obscene gesture.]
THE WITCH (laughs immoderately). Ha, ha! That’s your way. You’re the same mad rogue as ever.
MEPHISTOPHELES (to Faust). My friend, pay attention to this. This is how to deal with witches.
THE WITCH. Now, gentlemen — what’s your pleasure?
MEPHISTOPHELES. A good glass of the well-known juice! I must ask you to make it the oldest. Years double its strength.

THE WITCH. Most willingly! Here is a bottle I sometimes sip from myself — it no longer stinks in the slightest. I’ll give you a glass with pleasure. (Whispering.) But if this man drinks it unprepared, you know very well he can’t live an hour.

MEPHISTOPHELES. He’s a dear friend of mine — it’ll do him good. I don’t grudge him the best of your kitchen. Draw your circle, speak your spells, and give him a full cup. [The witch, with strange gestures, draws a circle and places strange things in it. Meanwhile the glasses begin to ring, and the cauldron begins to sound and make music. Lastly, she fetches a great book and places the monkeys in the circle, where they serve her as a reading-desk and hold the torch. She beckons Faust to approach.]
FAUST (to Mephistopheles). But tell me — what’s to come of all this? This absurd apparatus, these frantic gestures, this disgusting jugglery — I know them of old, and I utterly detest them.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Pooh — that’s only foolery. Don’t be so fastidious. As a medic, she has to put on a little hocus-pocus, so the dose will work properly on you.
[He makes Faust enter the circle.]

THE WITCH (with strong emphasis, begins to declaim from the book). You must understand: of one make ten, and let two go, and three make even — then you are rich. Lose the four! Out of five and six — so says the witch — make seven and eight; then it’s done. And nine is one, and ten is none. That is the witch’s one-times-one.

FAUST. I know it well, my friend — the whole book sounds like this. I’ve wasted many an hour on it, for a downright contradiction remains equally mysterious to wise people and fools. My friend, the art is old and new. It has always been the way of every age, by three and one and one and three, to spread error instead of truth.
FAUST. My head is going to split — listening to a hundred thousand fools talk. MEPHISTOPHELES. Enough, enough, excellent Sibyl! Bring the bowl quickly, full to the brim.

MEPHISTOPHELES. It is far from finished, I know it well — the whole book is in this vein. I’ve wasted many an hour on it. A perfect contradiction stays equally mysterious to the wise and to fools. My friend, the art is old and new. It has always been the fashion to spread error instead of truth by three and one, and one and three. So they prattle and teach without stopping; who is going to bother himself about these dolts? Men tend to believe, when they only hear words, that there must be something in them.
THE WITCH (continues). The high power of knowledge, hidden from the whole world! And he who does not think — to him it is given; he has it without trouble.
FAUST. What nonsense is she reciting to us? My head is splitting! It’s as if I were hearing a hundred thousand idiots declaiming in full chorus.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Enough, enough, excellent Sibyl! Hand us your drink, and fill the cup to the brim without more ado — this draught will do my friend no harm. He’s a man of many grades, who has already taken many a good gulp. [The witch, with many ceremonies, pours the liquor into a cup; as Faust lifts it to his mouth, a light flame rises.] Down with it at once! Don’t stand hesitating. It’ll warm your heart soon enough. Are you hail-fellow-well-met with the devil, and afraid of fire? [The witch dissolves the circle — Faust steps out.] Now — away at once. You mustn’t rest.
THE WITCH. Much good may the draught do you!
MEPHISTOPHELES (to the witch). And if there’s anything I can do to please you — just mention it on Walpurgis Night.
THE WITCH. Here is a song! If you sing it now and then, it will have a particular effect on you.

MEPHISTOPHELES (to Faust). Come quickly — be guided. You absolutely must perspire, so the potent juice can penetrate through your whole frame. Afterwards I’ll teach you to appreciate noble idleness, and before long you’ll feel, with heartfelt delight, how Cupid stirs and leaps about.
FAUST. Let me just look one more moment in the glass. That female form was too, too lovely.
MEPHISTOPHELES. No, no — you’ll soon see the model of all womankind in flesh and blood. (Aside.) With this drink in your body, you’ll soon see a Helen in every woman.

chapters.title: Street
paragraphs: FAUST. Margaret (passing by).
FAUST. My pretty lady, may I take the liberty of offering you my arm and my escort?
MARGARET. I am neither a lady nor pretty, and I can find my own way home. [She frees herself and exits.]

FAUST. By heaven, this girl is lovely! I’ve never seen her like. She is so modest and virtuous — and a little sharp-tongued with it. The red of her lip, the light on her cheek — I shall never forget them as long as I live. The way she cast down her eyes is stamped deep on my heart, and how cutting her speech was — it was absolutely ravishing!
[MEPHISTOPHELES enters.]
FAUST. Listen — you must get me that girl.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Which one?
FAUST. The one who just passed by.

MEPHISTOPHELES. What, her? She’s just come from her confessor, who absolved her of every sin. I crept up close to the chair. She’s an innocent little thing who had next to nothing to bring to the confessional. I have no power over her.
FAUST. But she’s past fourteen!

MEPHISTOPHELES. You sound exactly like Jack Rake, who covets every sweet flower for himself and imagines there is no honour or favour that can’t be had for the plucking. But it doesn’t always work that way.

FAUST. My honourable schoolmaster, don’t plague me with your morality. And in a word, I tell you this: if that sweet young creature is not lying in my arms this very night, then by midnight our compact is over.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Consider what’s possible. I need a fortnight at least just to find an opportunity.
FAUST. If I had only seven clear hours, I wouldn’t need the devil’s help to seduce a child like that.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Now you’re almost talking like a Frenchman — but please don’t fret about it. What good is going straight to enjoyment? The delight is nothing like as great as when you’ve kneaded and shaped the doll on every side with all sorts of nonsense, as many an Italian story shows.
FAUST. But I have appetite enough without all that.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Now, seriously, and without offence, I’ll tell you once and for all: the lovely girl is not to be had in such a hurry. Nothing here can be taken by storm — we’ll have to use strategy.
FAUST. Get me something of the angel’s. Bring me to her resting-place. Get me a kerchief from her bosom, a garter for my love.
MEPHISTOPHELES. To prove how anxious I am to serve your passion — we won’t lose a moment. This very day I’ll bring you to her chamber.
FAUST. And shall I see her? Have her?
MEPHISTOPHELES. No. She’ll be at a neighbour’s. Meanwhile, alone and in her atmosphere, you can feast yourself to your heart’s content on coming joys.
FAUST. Can we go now? MEPHISTOPHELES. It is too early.
FAUST. Get me a present for her. [Exit.]
MEPHISTOPHELES. Presents already! Excellent! That’s the way to succeed! I know many a fine place and many a long-buried treasure. I’ll have to go and look them over.
[Exit.]

EVENING. A neat little room. Margaret braiding and binding up her hair. Whoever the gentleman was today — he certainly looked gallant, and he comes from a noble house. I could read that on his forehead — MEPHISTOPHELES, Faust.
MEPHISTOPHELES. In here — softly, only come in!
FAUST (after a pause). Please, leave me alone.
FAUST (looking up). You who weave through this sanctuary! You who live languishing on the dew of hope! What a sense of order and contentment! In this little prison, what blessedness!
[He throws himself on the leather chair by the bed.]

chapters.title: Evening
paragraphs: A neat little room.

MARGARET (braiding and binding up her hair). I’d give something to know who that gentleman was today! He carried himself gallantly, and I’m sure he’s from a noble family — I could read it on his brow. Otherwise he wouldn’t have been so bold. [Exit.] MEPHISTOPHELES — FAUST.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Come in — softly, as quietly as you can. Just come in!
FAUST (after a pause). Leave me alone, I beg you.
MEPHISTOPHELES (prying about). Not every maiden keeps things this neat. [Exit.]

FAUST (looking round). Welcome, sweet twilight that pervades this sanctuary! Possess my heart, you delicious pangs of love who live languishing on the dew of hope! What a feeling of peace, order, and contentment breathes here! What abundance in this poverty! What bliss in this little cell! [He throws himself onto the leather chair beside the bed.] Oh, receive me — you who have welcomed, with open arms, in joy and sorrow, the generations now gone. How often a swarm of children must have clustered around this patriarch’s throne! Here, perhaps, in gratitude for her Christmas gift, my beloved, with the warm round cheek of childhood, kissed her grandfather’s withered hand. Maiden, I feel your spirit of order and abundance breathing around me — the spirit that teaches you daily like a mother, that tells you to spread the cloth neatly on the table and even curl the sand at your feet. Dear hand, so godlike — you make a hut into heaven. And here — [he lifts the bed curtain] — what a blissful tremor seizes me! Here I could linger for whole hours. Nature, you shaped this angel from birth, here, in airy dreams. Here the child lay, her gentle bosom filled with warm life. And here, with weavings of hallowed purity, the divine image unfolded. And you — what brought you here? How deeply moved I feel! What are you doing here? Why does your heart grow so heavy? Miserable Faust — I no longer know you. Am I in an enchanted atmosphere? I burned for instant enjoyment, and now I feel myself dissolving into a dream of love. Are we the sport of every breath of air? And if she walked in this very moment — how would you atone for your guilt? The big boaster — how small he’d be! Melted away at her feet.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Quick! I see her coming below.
FAUST. Away! Away! I will never come back!
MEPHISTOPHELES. I picked this up elsewhere. Just set it here in the press, to win some other girl over later. After all, a child is a child, and a game is a game.
FAUST. I don’t know — should I?

MEPHISTOPHELES. Why ask so much? Surely you don’t mean to keep the treasure for yourself? I hope you’re not turning miserly. [He closes the lock again.] Now — quick, away! To bend the dear girl to your heart’s desire. And there you stand looking as though Physics and Metaphysics were towering grey and bodily before you. Away! [Exit.]
MARGARET (with a lamp). It feels so close, so stuffy here. [She opens the window.] And yet it isn’t really warm outside. I’m beginning to feel — I don’t know how. I wish my mother would come home.
FAUST. Away! Away! I will return no more.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Here is a fairly heavy casket — I took it from somewhere else. Just place it here in the press at once. I swear to you, she’ll be quite beside herself. I put the trinkets in it to win another girl with — but a child is a child, and a game is a game.
FAUST. I don’t know — should I?

MEPHISTOPHELES. Is that a thing to ask? Are you thinking of keeping the treasure for yourself? In that case I’d advise your covetousness to spare these precious hours and spare me further trouble. I hope you’re not avaricious. I scratch my head, I rub my hands. [He places the casket in the press and closes the lock.] But away, quick — to bend the sweet young creature to your heart’s desire. And now you look as if you were going to a lecture-room, as if Physics and Metaphysics were standing there grey and bodily before you. Away! [Exeunt.]

MARGARET (with a lamp). It feels so close, so sultry here. [She opens the window.] And yet outside isn’t really so warm. I’m beginning to feel I don’t know how. I wish my mother would come home. I’m trembling all over — but I’m a silly, timid woman. [She begins to sing as she undresses.] SONG. There was a king in Thule, faithful unto the grave, to whom his dying mistress gave a golden goblet. He valued nothing above it; he emptied it at every feast; his eyes overflowed each time he drank from it. And when his time came to die, he counted up the cities of his kingdom and grudged none of them to his heir — but not so the goblet. He sat at the royal banquet, his knights around him, in the proud ancestral hall, there in his castle by the sea. There the old reveller stood, took a parting draught of life’s glow, and threw the hallowed goblet down into the waves. He saw it splash, fill, and sink deep into the sea; his eyes sank too, and he never drank a drop more. [She opens the press to put away her clothes, and notices the casket.] How did this beautiful casket get here? I’m certain I locked the press. How strange! What can be in it? Perhaps someone brought it as a pledge, and my mother lent money on it. A little key hangs by the ribbon — I’ve half a mind to open it. What is this? Good heavens — look! I have never in my life seen anything like it! A set of jewels! A noble lady might wear such things on the highest feast day. How would the chain look on me?
[She adorns herself with them and steps before the looking-glass.]

If only the earrings were mine! One cuts quite a different figure in them. What does your beauty or youth count for? It may all be pretty and good, but people pass it by. They praise you, half in pity. After gold everyone presses — on gold everything depends. Alas, we poor ones!

chapters.title: Promenade
paragraphs: Faust walks up and down, deep in thought. MEPHISTOPHELES enters.
MEPHISTOPHELES. By all rejected love! By the flames of hell! I wish I knew something worse to swear by!
FAUST. What is the matter? What is pinching you so hard? I’ve never seen such a face in my life!
MEPHISTOPHELES. I could hand myself over to the devil this minute, if I weren’t a devil already.
FAUST. Is your brain out of joint? It suits you, truly, to rave like a madman.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Just think of it! A priest has carried off the jewels meant for Margaret. The mother caught sight of the thing and at once felt a secret horror of it. The woman has a fine nose, truly — she’s forever sniffing through her prayer book, and she can smell on any piece of furniture whether it’s holy or profane. She plainly smelled out in the jewels that there was no blessing in them. “My child,” she said, “unrighteous wealth ensnares the soul and consumes the blood. We shall consecrate it to the Mother of God; she will gladden us with heavenly manna!” Margaret pulled a sour face — after all, she thought, it’s a gift horse, and the man who brought it so handsomely can hardly be godless. The mother sent for a priest. The moment he heard the curious story, the look of it pleased him greatly. He said: “This shows a good disposition. He who conquers himself is the true victor. The church has a strong stomach — she has swallowed whole countries and never yet eaten herself sick. The church alone, my good women, can digest unrighteous wealth.”
FAUST. That’s a common enough trick — a Jew and a king can do it too.

MEPHISTOPHELES. So saying, he swept off clasp, chain, and ring as if they were trifles, thanked them no more and no less than if it had been a basket of nuts, promised them all heavenly reward — and they were greatly edified.
FAUST. And Margaret?

MEPHISTOPHELES. She is sitting now in restless misery, not knowing what she wants or what to do with herself, thinking day and night about the trinkets, and even more about the man who brought them. FAUST. My love’s grief distresses me. Get her another set at once. The first was no great matter, after all.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Oh, of course — it’s all child’s play to the gentleman!
FAUST. Do it, and arrange it the way I want. Stick close to her neighbour. Don’t be a milk-and-water devil — fetch a fresh set of jewels.
MEPHISTOPHELES. With all my heart, honoured sir. [Faust exits.]
MEPHISTOPHELES. A love-sick fool like this would puff sun, moon, and stars into the air just to amuse his mistress. [Exit.]

chapters.title: The Neighbour's House
paragraphs: MARTHA (alone). God forgive my dear husband — he hasn’t treated me well. He goes off straight into the world and leaves me here, all alone on the straw. And yet truly I never did anything to upset him. God knows I loved him with all my heart. [She weeps.] Perhaps he is actually dead! Oh, the torture! — If only I had a death certificate! MARGARET enters.
MARGARET. Dame Martha!
MARTHA. What’s the matter, Margaret?
MARGARET. My knees can hardly hold me up! I’ve found another casket of ebony in my press — exactly like the first, only with things much grander, far costlier.
MARTHA. You mustn’t say a word about this to your mother. She’d carry it straight off to the confessional again.
MARGARET. Now look — only look at them!
MEPHISTOPHELES (aside, to her). I know you now — that’s enough. You’ve a visitor of distinction here. Forgive the liberty. I’ll call again in the afternoon.
MARTHA (aloud). Just think, child — of all things! This gentleman takes you for a lady.
MARGARET. I’m only a poor young thing. Oh, sir, you are too kind. The jewels and ornaments are not mine.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Ah — it isn’t the jewels alone. You have a bearing, a look, so striking. How glad I am that I may stay.
MARTHA. What is it you bring, then? I’m most curious —
MEPHISTOPHELES. I wish I had better news! I hope you won’t make me suffer for it. Your husband is dead, and sends his greetings.
MARTHA. Dead? The poor soul! Oh, woe is me! My husband, dead! I shall die!
MARGARET. Oh, dear Dame, don’t despair.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Listen to the sad tale.
MARGARET. That’s why I should wish never to be in love as long as I live. The loss would grieve me to death.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Joy must have sorrow — sorrow, joy.
MARTHA. Tell me how his life ended.
MEPHISTOPHELES. He lies buried at St. Anthony’s in Padua, in well-consecrated ground, for an eternally cool bed of rest.

MARTHA. Have you nothing else for me? MEPHISTOPHELES. Yes — one request, big and heavy: be sure to have three hundred masses sung for him. As for the rest, my pockets are empty. MARTHA. What — not a medal? Not a keepsake? The sort of thing every journeyman saves at the bottom of his bag, keeping it as a token — going hungry, even begging, rather than parting with it —
MEPHISTOPHELES. Madam, I’m very sorry. But he really hasn’t squandered his money. He also bitterly repented his sins — and bewailed his bad luck even more.
MARGARET. Ah, that mortals should be so unfortunate! I shall certainly say many a prayer for his soul.
MEPHISTOPHELES. You deserve to be married right away. You’re a lovable child.
MARGARET. Oh no — that wouldn’t do for the present.
MEPHISTOPHELES. If not a husband, then a sweetheart in the meantime. It’s one of the best gifts of heaven, to have so sweet a thing in your arms.
MARGARET. That’s not the custom in this country.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Custom or not — such things do happen.
MARTHA. Tell me more!

MEPHISTOPHELES. I stood at his deathbed. It was something better than dung — half-rotten straw. But he died like a Christian, and found he still had a great deal on his account. “How thoroughly,” he cried, “must I despise myself — to have run away from my business and my wife like that. Oh, the memory is death to me. If only she would forgive me in this life!”
MARTHA (weeping). The good man! I forgave him long ago.
MEPHISTOPHELES. But, God knows, she was more to blame than I was.
MARTHA. He lied, then! What — telling lies on the brink of the grave!

MEPHISTOPHELES. He certainly fabled with his last breath, if I’m any judge. “I,” said he, “had no time to gape and idle — I had to make children first, and then bread for them — and bread in the widest sense — and couldn’t even eat my share in peace.”
MARTHA. Did he forget all my faithfulness, all my love — my drudgery day and night?

MEPHISTOPHELES. Not at all — he thought of it with affection. He said: “When I left Malta, I prayed fervently for my wife and children, and heaven was so far favourable that our ship captured a Turkish vessel carrying a treasure of the great sultan. Bravery had its reward, and, as was only right, I got my fair share.”
MARTHA. How? Where? Could he have buried it?

MEPHISTOPHELES. Who knows where it’s scattered now to the four winds of heaven! A pretty girl took an interest in him as he was wandering, a stranger, around Naples. She was so kind and faithful to him that he felt it right up to his blessed end.

MARTHA. The villain! Robbing his own children! And all the wretchedness, all the poverty, couldn’t check his scandalous life. MEPHISTOPHELES. But you see — he died of it. Now, if I were in your place, I’d mourn him a chaste year, and look about for a new sweetheart in the meantime.

MARTHA. Oh, God — but in this world I won’t easily find another like my first. There could hardly have been a sweeter little fool. He only loved roaming about a bit too much — and foreign women, and foreign wine, and the cursed dice.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Well, well — things might have gone on very well, if he, for his part, had only shown the same indulgence to you. I swear, on those terms, I would change rings with you myself!
MARTHA. Oh, the gentleman is pleased to jest.
MEPHISTOPHELES (aside). Now it’s high time to be off. She’d take the devil himself at his word. — (To Margaret.) How is your heart these days?
MARGARET. What do you mean, sir?
MEPHISTOPHELES (aside). Good, innocent child. — (Aloud.) Farewell, ladies!
MARGARET. Farewell!

MARTHA. Oh, but tell me quickly! I’d like to have a certificate showing where, how, and when my love died and was buried. I’ve always been a friend to order, and I’d like to read his death in the weekly paper.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Yes, my good madam — the truth is established by the testimony of two witnesses, all the world over. And I have a fine companion whom I’ll bring before the judge for you. I’ll fetch him here.
MARTHA. Oh, please do!
MEPHISTOPHELES. And the young lady will be here too? A fine fellow! Has travelled widely, and shows every politeness to the ladies.
MARGARET. I would be quite covered with confusion in his presence.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Not in the presence of any king on earth.
MARTHA. Behind the house, in my garden — we’ll expect you both this evening.

chapters.title: Street (II)
paragraphs: Faust — MEPHISTOPHELES.
FAUST. How does it go? Is it under way? Will it be done soon?

MEPHISTOPHELES. Bravo! Do I find you all on fire? Margaret will be yours very shortly. This evening you’ll see her at her neighbour Martha’s. The woman is practically tailor-made for the procuress and gypsy calling.
FAUST. So far, so good.
MEPHISTOPHELES. But something is required of us.
FAUST. One good turn deserves another.
MEPHISTOPHELES. We have only to swear a formal statement that her husband’s stiff limbs rest in consecrated ground at Padua.
FAUST. A clever scheme! I suppose we’ll first have to make the journey there.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Sancta simplicitas! No need for that. Just bear witness without knowing anything about the matter.
FAUST. If you have nothing better to suggest, the plan is finished.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Oh, holy man! There you go! Is this the first time in your life you’ve borne false witness? Haven’t you confidently laid down definitions of God, of the world, and of whatever moves in it — of man and the workings of his head and heart — with an unblushing face and a fearless breast? And if you look honestly at the real nature of things, you’ll have to admit you knew as much about those matters as you do about Mr. Schwerdtlein’s death!
FAUST. You are and always will be a liar and a sophist.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Yes — unless one looks a little deeper. Tomorrow, in all good faith, won’t you go and make a fool of poor Margaret, and swear to love her with your whole soul?
FAUST. And truly from my heart.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Fine words! And then you’ll speak of eternal faith and love — of one all-conquering, exclusive passion. Will that come from the heart as well?

FAUST. Quiet! It will! When I feel it, and search for a name for the passion, the frenzy, and find none — when I range with all my senses through the world, reaching for the loftiest expressions, and call this flame that consumes me endless, eternal, eternal — is that a devilish play of lies?
MEPHISTOPHELES. All the same, I am right.

FAUST. Listen — mark this, I beg you, and spare my lungs. Anyone who is determined to be right and has nothing but a tongue will undoubtedly be right. But come — I’m tired of arguing. You are right, especially because I can’t help myself.
MARGARET. He is so coarse, so rough!
MARTHA. And you, sir, are always travelling like this? MEPHISTOPHELES. Ah, that business and duty drive us to it! And we cannot stay, however much we’d wish.

chapters.title: Garden
paragraphs: MARGARET on Faust's arm, MARTHA with MEPHISTOPHELES, walking up and down.

MARGARET. I feel it, I really do — the gentleman is only being kind to me, only condescending so I'll blush. Travelers are used to putting up with whatever comes their way out of good nature. I know perfectly well that my poor chatter cannot entertain a man of your experience.
FAUST. One glance, one word from you gives greater pleasure than all the wisdom of this world.
[He kisses her hand.]
MARGARET. Don't trouble yourself! How can you kiss it? It is so coarse, so rough. The work I've had to do — heaven knows what — and my mother is so strict.
[They pass on.]
MARTHA. And you, sir, are always traveling like this?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Alas, that business and duty should drive us to it! How many a place one leaves with regret, and yet cannot stay in!

MARTHA. It does well enough in the wild years of youth to roam freely through the world. But the bad day comes at last, and to creep into the grave a solitary old bachelor — that has never done anyone any good. MEPHISTOPHELES. I shudder at the distant view of it. MARTHA. Then, worthy sir, think better of it while there is still time.
[They pass on.]
MARGARET. Yes, out of sight, out of mind! You wear your politeness easily. But you have plenty of friends, and they are wiser than I am.
FAUST. Oh dearest, believe me, what people call wise often better deserves the name of vanity and narrow-mindedness.
MARGARET. How so?
FAUST. Alas, that simplicity, that innocence, never appreciates itself or its own sacred worth! That humility, that lowliness — the highest gifts of generous, loving nature —
MARGARET. Only think of me for one little moment; I shall have time enough to think of you.
FAUST. You are much alone, I imagine?

MARGARET. Yes, our household is small, and yet it has to be looked after. We keep no maid. I have to cook, sweep, knit and sew, and run errands early and late. And my mother is so particular about everything! Not that she has any pressing need to economize. We could afford more than many others. My father left us a nice little property — a small house and a garden outside the town. Still, my days at the moment are reasonably quiet. My brother is a soldier; my little sister is dead. I had my full share of trouble with her, but I would gladly take all that worry on myself again — the child was so dear to me.
FAUST. An angel, if she was like you!

MARGARET. I raised her, and she loved me dearly. She was born after my father's death. We thought we'd lost my mother, the state she was in then; and she recovered very slowly, by degrees. So she couldn't think of nursing the poor little baby, and I brought her up all by myself, with milk and water. She became my own that way. On my arm, in my lap, she smiled and kicked and grew.
FAUST. You must have felt the purest joy.

MARGARET. And many anxious hours, too. The little one's cradle stood at night by my bedside; she could scarcely stir before I was awake — now having to give her drink, now to take her into bed with me, now, when she wouldn't quiet down, to get up and walk up and down the room rocking her; and early in the morning, already at the wash-tub, then off to market and to the cooking — and so on, day after day. Under such conditions, sir, one isn't always in good spirits; but food and rest taste the better for it. [They pass on.]
MARTHA. The poor women have the worst of it. It's no easy matter to convert an old bachelor.
MEPHISTOPHELES. It only depends on someone like you to teach me better.
MARTHA. Tell me plainly, sir — have you never met anyone? Has your heart never settled anywhere?
MEPHISTOPHELES. The proverb says — one's own hearth and a good wife are worth pearls and gold.
MARTHA. I mean, have you never had any inclination?
MEPHISTOPHELES. I have generally been received very politely.
MARTHA. I meant to say — was your heart never seriously touched?
MEPHISTOPHELES. One should never dare to joke with women.
MARTHA. Ah, you don't understand me.
MEPHISTOPHELES. I'm heartily sorry for it. But I do understand — that you are very kind. [They pass on.]
FAUST. You recognized me again, you little angel, the moment I came into the garden?
MARGARET. Didn't you see it? I lowered my eyes. FAUST. And you forgive the liberty I took — my forwardness as you were leaving the cathedral recently?

MARGARET. I was flustered; such a thing had never happened to me before; no one could say anything bad of me. Alas, I thought, has he seen something bold, unmaidenly in your behavior? It seemed as if the thought suddenly struck him: “I need stand on no ceremony with this girl.” I must admit, I didn't know what was beginning to stir in your favor; but I was certainly very angry with myself for not being able to be more angry with you.
FAUST. Sweet love!
MARGARET. Wait a moment! [She plucks a star-flower and picks off the petals one after another.]
FAUST. What is that for? A nosegay?
MARGARET. No, only a game.
FAUST. What sort?
MARGARET. Go on! You will laugh at me. [She plucks off the petals and murmurs to herself.]
FAUST. What are you murmuring?
MARGARET (HALF ALOUD). He loves me — he loves me not!
FAUST. You angelic being!
MARGARET (CONTINUES). Loves me — not — loves me — not — (plucking off the last petal with delighted joy) — he loves me!
FAUST. Yes, my child. Let this flower-prophecy be a divine oracle to you. He loves you! Do you understand what that means? He loves you!
[He takes both her hands.]
MARGARET. I tremble all over.

FAUST. Oh, do not tremble. Let this look, this pressure of the hand, say to you what is unutterable — to give ourselves up wholly, and feel a bliss that must be eternal! Eternal! — its end would be despair! No, no end! no end! [MARGARET presses his hands, breaks away from him, and runs off. He stands a moment in thought, then follows her.]
MARTHA (APPROACHING). Night is coming on. MEPHISTOPHELES. Yes, and we'll be off.

MARTHA. I would ask you to stay longer, but this is far too wicked a place. You'd think no one had any other purpose or occupation than gaping at his neighbor's comings and goings. And one gets talked about no matter how one behaves. And our pair of lovers?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Have flown up the path over there. Wanton butterflies!
MARTHA. He seems fond of her.
MEPHISTOPHELES. And she of him. Such is the way of the world.

chapters.title: A Summer House
paragraphs: MARGARET runs in, gets behind the door, holds the tip of her finger to her lips, and peeps through the crack.
MARGARET. He's coming!
FAUST (ENTERING). Ah, you rogue, is this how you tease me? I've caught you at last. [He kisses her.]
MARGARET (EMBRACING HIM AND RETURNING THE KISS). Dearest! I love you from my heart!
[MEPHISTOPHELES knocks.]
FAUST (STAMPING). Who is there?
MEPHISTOPHELES. A friend.
FAUST. A brute.
MEPHISTOPHELES. It is time to part, I believe.
MARTHA (COMES UP). Yes, it is late, sir.
FAUST. May I not see you home?
MARGARET. My mother would — farewell!
FAUST. Must I go, then? Farewell!
MARTHA. Goodbye!
MARGARET. Until we meet again soon!
[Faust and MEPHISTOPHELES exit.]

MARGARET. Gracious God! How many things such a man can think about! I just stand there embarrassed in his presence, and say yes to everything! I am only a poor silly girl; I can't understand what he sees in me. [Exit.] FAUST alone.

FAUST. Sublime spirit, you gave me, gave me everything I asked for. You did not turn your face to me in fire for nothing. You permitted me not merely a cold, wondering visit, but to look as into the heart of a friend. And when the storm roars and creaks in the forest, you give me back to myself and to my own breast; and when the pure moon rises before my gaze, the silvery forms of the ancient world hover up and soften the austere pleasure of contemplation. Oh, that nothing perfect ever falls to a human being's lot — I feel that now. You gave me, along with this rapture...

chapters.title: Forest and Cavern
paragraphs: FAUST (ALONE). Sublime spirit! You gave me, gave me everything I prayed for. Not in vain did you turn your face to me in fire; you gave me glorious nature for a kingdom, with the power to feel her and enjoy her. You do not merely permit me a cold, wondering visit; you grant me to look into her profound depth, as into the heart of a friend. You pass the whole series of living things in review before me, and teach me to know my brothers in the silent wood, in the air, and in the water. And when the storm roars and groans in the forest, and the giant pine, hurling down its neighboring branches and trunks, sweeps crashing down — and the mountain thunders with a dead, hollow muttering at the fall — then you bear me off to the sheltered cave; then you show me to myself, and the deep mysterious wonders of my own breast reveal themselves. And when the clear moon, with its soothing influence, rises full in my view — from the rocky walls, out of the damp undergrowth, the silvery forms of past ages hover up to me, and soften the austere pleasure of contemplation. Oh, I feel now that nothing perfect falls to a human being's lot! Along with this rapture, which brings me nearer and nearer to the gods, you gave me the companion — whom I already cannot do without, even though, cold and insolent, he degrades me in my own eyes and turns your gifts to nothing with a breath. He kindles a wild fire in my breast for that lovely image. So I reel from desire to enjoyment, and in enjoyment I languish for desire. [MEPHISTOPHELES enters.]
MEPHISTOPHELES. It is well enough to try a thing once; but then on to something new again!
FAUST. I wish you had more to do than to plague me on a good day.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Now, now! I'll gladly let you rest — you needn't take it so seriously. In a companion as ungracious, harsh, and crazy as you, there is truly little to lose. FAUST. That is just the right tone! He even wants thanks for boring me.
MEPHISTOPHELES. From the crotchets of imagination I have at any rate cured you for a while; and but for me you would already have walked off this globe.

MEPHISTOPHELES. — whom I already cannot do without; though, cold and insolent, he degrades me in my own eyes and turns your gifts to nothing with a breath. He is forever kindling a wildfire in my heart for that lovely image. So I reel from desire to enjoyment, and in enjoyment languish for desire. [MEPHISTOPHELES enters.]
MEPHISTOPHELES. Haven't you had enough of this kind of life? How can you take delight in it for any length of time? It is well enough to try it once, but then on again to something new.
FAUST. I wish you had something else to do than to plague me in my happier hour.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Well, well! I will let you alone if you wish. You needn't say so in earnest. Truly, it is little to lose an ungracious, peevish, crazy companion like you. All day long one has one's hands full. One cannot read in your worship's face what pleases you and what to leave alone.
FAUST. That is just the right tone! He'd like to be thanked for boring me to death.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Poor son of earth! What sort of life would you have led without me? I have cured you, for some time to come, of the crotchets of imagination — and but for me you would already have taken your departure from this globe. Why mope in caverns and crevices of rock like an owl? Why suck nourishment from soggy moss and dripping stone like a toad? A fine, sweet pastime! The doctor still sticks in you.

FAUST. Do you understand what new life-force this wandering in the wilderness gives me? Yes, if you could even have a dim notion of it, you would be devil enough to begrudge me my enjoyment. MEPHISTOPHELES. A super-earthly pleasure! To lie on the mountains in darkness and dew — to embrace earth and heaven ecstatically — to swell yourself up into a godhead — to rake through the earth's marrow with your prophetic yearnings — to feel the whole six days' work in your breast — in haughty might to enjoy I know not what — now to overflow, in love's raptures, into all, with your earthly nature cast aside — and then to end the lofty intuition (with a gesture) — I must not say how.
FAUST. Shame on you.

MEPHISTOPHELES. That is not to your liking; you are entitled to cry shame, so morally! We must not name to chaste ears what chaste hearts cannot give up. And, in a word, I don't begrudge you the pleasure of lying to yourself occasionally. But you won't keep it up long. You are already worn out again, and if this goes on much longer, you'll be fretted into madness or into torment and horror. Enough of this! Your little love sits over there at home, and to her everything is cramped and melancholy. You are never absent from her thoughts. She loves you overwhelmingly. At first your passion came overflowing, like a stream swollen with melted snow; you poured it into her heart, and now your stream is dry again. I think, instead of holding court in the woods, your lordship would do well to reward the poor young creature for her love. The time seems wretchedly long to her; she stands at the window and watches the clouds roll away over the old town walls. “If I were a bird!” — so runs her song, all day long and half the night. Now she is cheerful, mostly downcast — now she has cried her fill — then, as it seems, calm again, and ever in love!
FAUST. Serpent! Serpent!
MEPHISTOPHELES (ASIDE). Now I have you!
FAUST. Reprobate! Take yourself away, and don't name the lovely woman. Don't bring the desire for her sweet body before my half-distracted senses again!
MEPHISTOPHELES. What is to become of this? She thinks you've gone off, and in a way you have.
FAUST. I am near her, and even were I ever so far off, I can never forget her, never lose her. Indeed, I already envy the body of the Lord when her lips are touching it.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Very well, my friend! I have often envied you the twin pair that grazes among the roses.
FAUST. Pander, be gone!

MEPHISTOPHELES. He has recognized the noblest calling — even to make opportunity itself. Away with you now! It is a great pity. You ought to be in your sweetheart's chamber, not, of all things, in death.

FAUST. What are the joys of heaven in her arms? Let me warm myself on her breast — and do I not always feel her wretchedness? Am I not the fugitive, the homeless one, the monster without purpose or rest, who, like a cataract, raged from rock to rock in devouring fury toward the precipice? And she, on the side, with childlike simplicity, in her little cottage on the little mountain field, all her homely cares embraced within that little world! And I, the God-hated one — it was not enough for me to grasp the rocks and smite them to shatters! Her, her peace, I had to undermine too! Hell, you had to have this sacrifice! Devil, help me to shorten the pang! Let what must be, be at once! Let her fate fall crushing upon me, and let her go to ruin together with me!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Very well, my friend! I have often envied you the twin pair which feeds among roses.
FAUST. Pander, be gone!

MEPHISTOPHELES. Good again! You rail, and I cannot help laughing. The God who made lad and lass well understood the noble calling of making opportunity too. But away — it is a fine thing to be sad about! You should betake yourself to your mistress's chamber, not, I think, to death.

FAUST. What are the joys of heaven in her arms? Even when I take fire on her breast, do I not feel her wretchedness without ceasing? Am I not the outcast — the homeless one — the monster without aim or rest, who, like a cataract, dashed from rock to rock in devouring fury toward the precipice? And she, beside it, with childlike simplicity, in her little cottage on the little mountain field, all her homely cares embraced within that little world! And I, the hated of God — it was not enough for me to grasp the rocks and smite them to shatters! Her, her peace, I had to undermine too! Hell, you could not rest without this sacrifice! Devil, help me to shorten the pang! Let what must be, be quickly! Let her fate fall crushing upon me, and let us both perish together!

MEPHISTOPHELES. How it seethes and glows again! Get in there and comfort her, you fool! When such a dull head sees no way out, it imagines at once that all is at an end. Long live the one who bears himself bravely! Well, on the whole, you have a fair spice of the devil in you. I know nothing in the world more insipid than a devil who despairs.

chapters.title: Margaret's Room
paragraphs:
MARGARET (ALONE, AT THE SPINNING-WHEEL).
My peace is gone,
My heart is heavy;
I shall find it never
And never more.

Where I have him not
Is the grave to me.
The whole world
Is embittered to me.

My poor head
Is wandering,
My poor sense
Distracted.

My peace is gone,
My heart is heavy;
I shall find it never
And never more.

For him alone I look
Out at the window;
For him alone I go
Out of the house.

His stately step,
His noble form,
The smile of his mouth,
The power of his eyes,

And of his speech
The bewitching flow,
The pressure of his hand,
And, ah, his kiss!

My peace is gone,
My heart is heavy;
I shall find it never
And never more.

My bosom yearns
Toward him.
Ah, could I clasp him
And hold him!

And kiss him
As I would!
Under his kisses
I should die away!

chapters.title: Martha's Garden
paragraphs: MARGARET—FAUST.
MARGARET. Promise me, Henry!
FAUST. Whatever I can!
MARGARET. Now, tell me, how is it with your religion? You are a dear, good man, but I believe you don't think much of it.
FAUST. Leave that, my child! You feel I love you: I would lay down my life for those I love, nor would I deprive anyone of their feeling and their church.
MARGARET. That is not right; we have to believe in it.
FAUST. Do we?
MARGARET. Ah, if only I had any influence over you! You don't honor the holy sacraments either.
FAUST. I honor them.
MARGARET. But without wanting them. It is a long time since you went to Mass or to confession. Do you believe in God?
FAUST. My love, who dares to say, “I believe in God”? You may ask priests and philosophers, and their answer will seem nothing but a mockery of the questioner.
MARGARET. So you don't believe?

FAUST. Don't misunderstand me, sweet darling! Who dares to name him? And who can profess, “I believe in him”? Who can feel — and dare to say, “I do not believe in him”? The All-embracer, the All-sustainer — does he not embrace and sustain you, me, himself? Does not the heaven arch itself there above? Does not the earth lie firm here below? And do the eternal stars not rise, twinkling kindly, on high? Are we not looking into each other's eyes, and isn't everything thronging into your head and heart, and weaving in eternal mystery — invisibly and visibly — around you? Fill your heart with it, big as it is, and when you are wholly blessed in the feeling, then call it what you will! Call it Bliss! — Heart! — Love! — God! I have no name for it! Feeling is everything. Name is sound and smoke, clouding heaven's glow.
MARGARET. That is all very fine and good. The priest says nearly the same thing, only in somewhat different words.
FAUST. All hearts in all places, under the blessed light of day, say it, each in its own language — why not I in mine?
MARGARET. When one hears it like this it seems passable; but for all that, there's something wrong about it, because you have no Christianity.
FAUST. Dear child!
MARGARET. I have long been troubled by the company I see you in.
FAUST. How so?
MARGARET. The man you have with you is hateful to me in my inmost soul. Nothing in the whole course of my life has given my heart such a pang as the repulsive face of that man.
FAUST. Don't be afraid of him, sweet love!
MARGARET. His presence makes my blood creep. I have kind feelings toward everyone else; but, much as I long —
MARGARET. Ah, if only I slept alone! I would gladly leave the door unbolted for you this very night. But my mother doesn't sleep soundly, and if she were to find us out, I should die on the spot.
FAUST. You angel, there's no fear of that. You see this little bottle! Just three drops in her drink will gently envelop her in deep sleep.
MARGARET. What would I not do for your sake? It won't do her any harm, I hope.
FAUST. Would I otherwise advise it to you, my love?

MARGARET. If, best of men, I do but look at you, I don't know what drives me to comply with your will. I have already done so much for you that scarcely anything more remains for me to do. [Exit.] MEPHISTOPHELES enters.
MEPHISTOPHELES. The little monkey! Is she gone?
FAUST. Have you been playing the spy again?

MEPHISTOPHELES. I heard what passed plainly enough. You were catechized, Doctor. Much good may it do you. The girls are certainly deeply interested in knowing whether a man is pious and simple-minded after the old fashion. They think, “If he is pliable in that matter, he will also obey us.”

FAUST. Monster as you are, you cannot conceive how this loving, faithful soul, full of her faith — which, according to her notions, is alone capable of conferring eternal happiness — feels a holy horror to think that she must consider her best-beloved lost.
MEPHISTOPHELES. You super-sensual, sensual lover — a slip of a girl leads you by the nose.
FAUST. You abortion of dirt and fire!

MEPHISTOPHELES. And she is shrewd in physiognomy too. In my presence she feels she knows not how. My little mask betokens some hidden meaning. She feels that I am most certainly a genius — perhaps the devil himself. Tonight, then — ?
FAUST. What is that to you?
MEPHISTOPHELES. I take my pleasure in it, all the same.

chapters.title: At the Well
paragraphs: MARGARET and BESSY with pitchers.
BESSY. Have you heard nothing about Barbara?
MARGARET. Not a word. I go out very little.
BESSY. It's true — Sybella told me today. She has finally made a fool of herself. That's what comes of playing the fine lady.
MARGARET. How so?
BESSY. It's a bad business. She feeds two now when she eats and drinks.
MARGARET. Ah!

BESSY. She is served right at last. What a time she has been hanging on that fellow! There was the strolling, the running off to village resorts and dance halls — she had to be the first one everywhere — he was always treating her to tarts and wine. She thought a great deal of her looks, and was so lost to honor she wasn't ashamed to take presents from him. There was hugging and kissing — and now the flower is gone!
MARGARET. Poor thing!

BESSY. You even pity her! When girls like us were at the spinning, our mothers never let us go out at night. She was with her sweet lover on the bench by the door and in the dark passage, and the time was never too long for them. But now she may humble herself and do church-penance in a sinner's smock, in front of the whole congregation.
MARGARET. He'll surely make her his wife. BESSY. He'd be a fool to do it. A lively young fellow has the world before him. Besides, he's gone.
MARGARET. That's not fair!
BESSY. If she gets him, it will go badly for her. The boys will tear her bridal wreath, and we'll strew chaff before her door. [Exit.]

MARGARET (GOING HOME). How fiercely I used to rail when I saw a poor girl make a slip! How I could never find words enough to speak of someone else's shame! How black it seemed to me — and I blackened it still more; it was never black enough for me — and I blessed myself and felt so grand, and now I myself am prey to sin! Yet — all that drove me to it was, God knows, so sweet, so dear!

chapters.title: Zwinger
paragraphs:
Oh, incline,
You full of pain,
The sword in your heart,
With a thousand pangs
You look up to your Son's death.
To the Father you look,
And send sighs aloft
For his and your distress.
The pain in my bones —
What my poor heart fears here,
What it trembles for, what it longs for,
You alone know, you alone!
Whichever way I go,
What woe, what woe, what woe
Grows in my bosom here!
I am scarcely ever alone — [In the niche of the wall a devotional image of the Mater Dolorosa, with pots of flowers before it.]

MARGARET (PLACES FRESH FLOWERS IN THE POTS).
Oh, incline,
You full of pain,
Your face graciously to my distress!

The sword in your heart,
With a thousand pangs,
You look up to your Son's death.

To the Father you look,
And send sighs aloft
For his and your distress.

Who feels
How it rages —
My torment to the quick?
How my poor heart throbs in me,
How it trembles, how it yearns —
You alone know, you alone!

Wherever I go,
What woe, what woe, what woe
Grows in my bosom here!
Hardly, alas, am I ever alone —
I weep, I weep, I weep,
My heart is breaking inside me.

The flower-pots on my window sill
I watered with tears, alas,
When at the dawn of morning
I plucked these flowers for you.

When brightly into my chamber
The rising sun's rays shone,
Already, in all wretchedness,
I was sitting up in my bed.

Help! Save me from shame and death!
Oh, incline,
You full of pain,
Your face graciously to my distress!

chapters.title: Night. Street before Margaret's Door
paragraphs: VALENTINE (A SOLDIER, MARGARET'S BROTHER). When I used to sit at some drinking party, where men love to brag, and my companions praised the loveliest girls and washed their compliments down with full cups, I would lean on the table with my elbows, sit there in quiet confidence, and listen to all their swaggering. Then I would stroke my beard with a smile, take the full cup in my hand, and say: 'All very well in its way! But is there one girl in the whole country to compare with my dear Margaret, one who is fit to hold a candle to my sister?' Cling, clang! the toasts went round! Some shouted, 'He is right! She is the pearl of the whole sex,' and all those braggarts were silenced. And now—it is enough to make a man tear out his hair by the roots and run up the walls—I have to endure every knave's sneer and taunt, sit like a bankrupt debtor, and sweat at every chance word that drops. And though I might crush them all with a single blow, still I could not call them liars. Who comes there? Who is slinking this way? If I am not mistaken, there are two of them. If it is he, I will attack him at once; he shall not leave this spot alive. [Enter FAUST and MEPHISTOPHELES.]

FAUST. Look how the light of the eternal lamp flickers up from the sacristy window, glimmers weaker and weaker along its edges, while darkness thickens around it. Just so is everything night-like within my own breast.

MEPHISTOPHELES. And I feel as languid as a tomcat that slinks along the fire-ladders and then creeps stealthily round the walls. I feel quite virtuous—with a touch of thievish pleasure, a touch of wantonness. The glorious Walpurgis Night already tingles through every limb of mine. The day after tomorrow it comes round again, and then a man knows what he wakes for.

FAUST. Will that treasure I see glimmering yonder rise to the surface in the meantime? MEPHISTOPHELES. You shall soon have the pleasure of lifting the kettle out. I took a glance at it the other day. There are splendid lion-dollars inside.
FAUST. Not a trinket, not a ring, to adorn my lovely mistress with?
MEPHISTOPHELES. I believe I saw something of that sort there—a kind of pearl necklace.
FAUST. Good. It pains me to go to her without a gift.

MEPHISTOPHELES. You should not begrudge yourself an enjoyment that costs nothing. Now that the sky is thick with stars, you shall hear a true masterpiece. I will sing her a moral song, the more surely to lure her in. [He sings to the guitar.] 'What are you doing here, Catherine, before your lover's door at the break of dawn? Stay, and beware! He lets you in a maid—not to come out a maid. Beware! Once it is done, then good night to you, you poor, poor things. If you love yourselves, do nothing to please any spoiler, except with the ring on your finger.'
VALENTINE (COMES FORWARD). Whom are you luring here? A plague on you, you cursed rat-catcher! First, to the devil with the instrument—then to the devil with the singer!
MEPHISTOPHELES. The guitar is broken to pieces! It is all up with it.
VALENTINE. Now for a skull-cracking!
MEPHISTOPHELES (TO FAUST). Don't give way, Doctor! Courage! Stay close, and do as I tell you. Out with your blade! Thrust away, and I will parry.
VALENTINE. Parry that!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Why not?
VALENTINE. And that!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Of course. VALENTINE. I believe the devil himself is fighting me. What is this? My hand is already crippled.
MEPHISTOPHELES (TO FAUST). Thrust home!
VALENTINE (FALLS). Oh, the torture!
MEPHISTOPHELES. The lout is tamed now. But away! We must vanish in an instant, for already a fearful outcry is rising. I can manage the police well enough, but the law of blood is another matter.
MARTHA (AT THE WINDOW). Out, out!
MARGARET (AT THE WINDOW). Bring a light!
MARTHA (AS BEFORE). They are cursing and scuffling, screaming and fighting. PEOPLE. Here lies one dead already.
MARTHA (COMING OUT). Have the murderers escaped?
MARGARET (COMING OUT). Who lies here? PEOPLE. Your mother's son. MARGARET. Almighty God! What misery!

VALENTINE. I am dying—that is soon said, and sooner still done. Why do you women stand there howling and wailing? Come here and listen to me. [All gather round him.] Look here, my little Margaret! You are still young, you are not yet shrewd enough, and you manage your matters badly. Let me say it in confidence—since you have become a whore once for all, then be one in good earnest.
MARGARET. Brother! God! What do you mean?

VALENTINE. Leave the Lord God out of this game. What is done, alas, cannot be undone, and things will run their course. You began in secret with one; soon more will follow, and when a dozen have had you, the whole town will have you too. When Shame is first born, she is brought into the world in secret, and the veil of night is drawn close over her head and ears. People would gladly smother her. But when she grows and swells, she walks flaunting in broad daylight, and yet she is no fairer for it. The uglier her face becomes, the more she courts the light of day. Indeed, I can already see the time when every honest townsman will turn aside from you, you harlot, as from an infected corpse. Your heart will sink within you when they look you in the face. You will wear no golden chain again! No more will you stand at the altar in church, or take pride in a fine lace collar at the dance. You will hide yourself in some dark, miserable corner, among beggars and cripples, and even if God forgives you, you will be cursed upon earth!
MARTHA. Commend your soul to God's mercy. Will you heap the sin of slander upon it too?
VALENTINE. If I could only lay hands on your withered body, you shameless bawd, I should hope to win full pardon for all my sins!
MARGARET. My brother! Oh, this agonizing pang!
VALENTINE. Have done with tears, I tell you. When you gave up honour, you struck the deepest blow into my heart. I go through the sleep of death to God, a soldier, and a brave one. [He dies.]

chapters.title: Cathedral
paragraphs: [A service in progress, organ and anthem. MARGARET among a crowd of people. An EVIL SPIRIT stands behind MARGARET.]

EVIL SPIRIT. How different it was for you, Margaret, when you still came to that altar full of innocence—when you lisped your prayers from the worn little book, half a child at play, half with God in your heart! Margaret! Where is your head? Inside your heart, what crime lies hidden? Are you praying for your mother's soul—the soul that slept over into long, long suffering because of you? Whose blood is on your threshold? And under your heart, does it not stir, quickening even now, tormenting itself and you with its waiting presence?
MARGARET. Woe! Woe! If only I could be free of the thoughts that come over me and rise up against myself!
CHORUS. Dies irae, dies illa, solvet saeclum in favilla. [The organ plays.]
EVIL SPIRIT. Horror seizes you! The Trumpet sounds! The graves tremble! And your heart, dragged from the rest of its ashes back into fiery torment, shudders awake!
MARGARET. If only I were away from here! I feel as if the organ were smothering my breath, as if the anthem were dissolving the very core of my heart!
CHORUS. Judex ergo cum sedebit, quidquid latet, apparebit, nil inultum remanebit.
MARGARET. I feel so crushed! The wall-pillars are closing in on me! The vaulted roof is bearing down on me—Air!
EVIL SPIRIT. Hide yourself! Sin and shame cannot be hidden. Air? Light? Woe to you!
CHORUS. Quid sum miser tunc dicturus? Quem patronum rogaturus, cum vix justus sit securus?
EVIL SPIRIT. The blessed turn their faces away from you. The pure shudder at the thought of reaching out their hands to you. Woe!
CHORUS. Quid sum miser tunc dicturus?
MARGARET. Neighbour! Your smelling bottle!
[She faints.]

chapters.title: Walpurgis-Night
paragraphs: [THE HARTZ MOUNTAINS. District of Schierke and Elend.]
[FAUST. MEPHISTOPHELES.]
MEPHISTOPHELES. Don't you long for a broomstick? For my part, I'd be glad of even the sturdiest he-goat. By this road we're still far from where we're going.

FAUST. So long as my legs feel fresh, this knotted stick is enough for me. What is the use of cutting the way short? To creep through the labyrinth of the valleys, and then to climb these rocks where the ever-bubbling spring comes tumbling down—that is the pleasure that gives such a path its zest. Spring is already stirring in the birch trees, and even the pine is beginning to feel it. Should it not have some effect on our limbs too?

MEPHISTOPHELES. Truly, I feel none of it. Everything in my body is wintry, and I'd much rather have frost and snow on my path. How mournfully the imperfect red moon rises with its belated glare, giving so poor a light that at every step you bump into a tree or a rock. With your permission, I'll call a will-o'-the-wisp. I see one over there, burning merrily away. Hello there, my friend! May I beg your company? Why do you blaze away so uselessly? Be so good as to light us along here. WILL-O'-THE-WISP. Out of respect, I hope, I shall manage to subdue my unsteady nature; our course is usually nothing but a zigzag. MEPHISTOPHELES. Ha! Ha! You're trying to imitate human beings, are you? But go straight, in the devil's name, or I'll blow your flickering life out. WILL-O'-THE-WISP. I see clearly you are master of the house, and I'll gladly accommodate myself to you. But consider! The mountain is magic-mad tonight, and if a will-o'-the-wisp is to show you the way, you mustn't be too particular. [FAUST, MEPHISTOPHELES, WILL-O'-THE-WISP, in alternating song.] We have entered, it seems, the realm of dreams and enchantments. Lead us right, and do yourself credit, that we may quickly advance into these wide, desolate regions. See how the trees go rushing past one after another, and the cliffs that bow down, and the long-snouted rocks—how they snort, how they blow! Through the stones, through the turf, brook and brooklet come hurrying down. Do I hear a rustling? Do I hear songs? Do I hear the sweet lament of love—voices of those blessed days? What we hope, what we love! And Echo, like a tale from olden times, sends the sound back. Tu-whit! Tu-whoo! It sounds nearer; the screech-owl, the plover, and the jay—have they all stayed awake? Are those salamanders moving through the bushes, with their long legs and thick bellies? And the roots, like snakes, wind out of rock and sand and stretch forth strange tendrils to terrify us and seize us; from living, gnarled trunks they push out polyp-fibres toward the wanderer. And the mice, in their thousand colours and whole tribes, scurry through the moss and through the heath! And the glow-worms fly in crowded swarms, a bewildering escort. But tell me, are we standing still or moving on? Everything seems to turn around—the rocks and trees making grimaces, and the will-o'-the-wisps multiplying, swelling themselves out.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Keep a firm hold on my coat-tail! Here is a central peak, from which you can see with wonder how Mammon is glowing in the mountain.

FAUST. How strangely a melancholy light, like a red dawn, glimmers through the mountain gorges and quivers down even into the deepest folds of the abyss! Here vapours rise, there exhalations drift; here sparks glow out of mist and haze, then steal along like a fine thread, then burst out again like a fountain. Here it winds its way for a long stretch with a hundred veins through the valley, and here, in some narrow corner, it suddenly scatters. There sparks are sputtering nearby, like scattered grains of golden sand. But look! The wall of rocks is on fire along its whole height.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Doesn't Sir Mammon light up his palace magnificently for this festival? Lucky for you that you've seen it. I can already feel the approach of the boisterous guests.
FAUST. How the storm-blast is raging through the air! What thumps it deals against my neck!
